quiz.stem: An invoice-extraction agent runs a hand-written Messages API loop that exits as soon as the first content block of a response has type text. About one invoice in twelve ends with no extracted record and no error. The transcripts for those runs show a final response containing a short text block such as "Let me check the vendor master first" followed by a tool_use block. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The max_tokens limit is too low, so those responses are truncated before the extraction tool call completes.
The loop checks content block types, not stop_reason, so it exits on a tool_use turn and drops the call.
The vendor-master tool is returning an empty result, and the model reads that result as a signal to stop working.
The loop has no turn cap, so the batch runner terminates long runs before the extraction tool is ever called.
quiz.explanation: A single response can carry a text block and a tool_use block together, and the stop_reason on that response is tool_use, meaning Claude is waiting for a result. Breaking on the first text block ends the loop mid-task without any error, which matches the silent missing records. The fix is to branch on stop_reason: continue on tool_use and handle every other value explicitly.

quiz.stem: An internal engineering research assistant uses a server-side web search tool inside a Messages API loop. The loop continues only while stop_reason is tool_use and returns the text for any other value. On broad questions, users receive answers that stop mid-thought with no error, and the logs show stop_reason pause_turn on the final response. Which change fixes this with the least added cost?
options: Raise max_tokens so the model has enough output budget to finish its answer in a single response.
Treat pause_turn like a refusal, read stop_details, and retry the same request on a fallback model.
On pause_turn, append the assistant content and send another request to continue the same turn.
Raise the loop's turn cap so the server-side search tool is allowed more iterations before it stops.
quiz.explanation: pause_turn means a server-tool loop reached its iteration limit (default ten) and the turn is not finished; it is a continuation point, not a completion. Sending the assistant content back resumes the same turn, so the answer completes without redoing earlier work. Code that treats everything except tool_use as an exit abandons that work silently.

quiz.stem: A contract-extraction pipeline processes merger document bundles of several hundred pages in one conversation. On the largest bundles the final response arrives with stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded, and the partial JSON has been quietly stored as if complete. The team proposes doubling max_tokens. Which change actually addresses the failure?
options: Double max_tokens as proposed, so the model has room to emit the full JSON record for the largest bundles.
Retry the same request at a lower temperature so the model produces a more compact JSON representation.
Treat the response as complete but run a JSON repair step that closes any unterminated arrays or objects.
Mark it truncated, then compact the context or move per-document extraction into fresh subagents.
quiz.explanation: model_context_window_exceeded is truncation caused by the model's context window being full, not by the output limit, so raising max_tokens cannot help. The response must be marked truncated rather than parsed, and the work restructured so each piece fits: compaction, summarization, or per-document subagents that each start with a fresh window.

quiz.stem: A refund agent's loop has a turn cap of 30 and exits on end_turn. Two problems appear in production: some cases are logged as resolved although no refund was issued and no escalation ticket exists, and some runs call lookup_order with identical arguments over and over until the turn cap fires. Leadership wants both failure classes caught without raising cost. Which two changes should the architect make? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a system prompt sentence telling the agent not to finish until the customer's issue is fully resolved.
Have code verify that a refund id or escalation ticket exists before any case is logged as resolved.
Raise the turn cap to 60 so that the repeated lookups have room to eventually reach a useful result.
Scan the agent's final reply for the word "resolved" and treat its presence as confirmation of success.
Hash each tool name plus arguments, and halt after a bounded run of turns with no new call signature.
quiz.explanation: end_turn means the model stopped talking, not that the task succeeded, so only an acceptance check your code evaluates can separate resolved from abandoned. The repeated identical lookups are a busy-but-stuck loop that a turn cap merely bounds; no-progress detection on duplicate call signatures stops it early and cheaply. Each guard catches a failure the other cannot.

quiz.stem: To cut token spend, an engineer changes a hand-written coding agent's loop so that after each tool call it appends only the user message holding the tool_result, and skips the assistant message that held the tool_use block. Requests immediately start failing with API errors on the second iteration. What is the correct explanation and fix?
options: The API is stateless, so each request must carry the assistant tool_use message followed by a matching tool_result.
The API remembers the assistant turn server-side, so the errors come from a stale session id that must be refreshed.
The tool_result lacks is_error set to false, so the API cannot tell whether the call succeeded and rejects it.
The max_tokens value is too low for the second request, so it must be raised to fit the added tool output.
quiz.explanation: The Messages API keeps no state between calls; your loop owns the history and must send it in full. Each tool_result must reference a tool_use id from the immediately preceding assistant message, so removing that message orphans the result, which is an API error rather than a degraded answer. Token savings have to come from elsewhere, such as trimming tool output.

quiz.stem: A pull-request review agent in CI runs a loop of the form "while iterations < 6", and when the counter reaches six it posts whatever it has as the finished review. Small pull requests finish in three iterations; large ones are routinely cut off and their partial reviews are posted as complete. The team wants accurate reviews without unbounded runs. Which change is best?
options: Raise the counter to 30 so that large pull requests have enough iterations to finish their reviews.
Remove the counter entirely and rely on end_turn as the only way the review loop is allowed to exit.
Make stop_reason the primary exit and keep the counter as a safety valve that marks the run halted.
Have the agent end each review with "REVIEW COMPLETE" and exit the loop when that phrase appears.
quiz.explanation: An iteration cap is a circuit breaker, not a termination condition: used as the primary stop it wastes calls on small tasks and cuts large ones off. The primary exit should be the structured stop_reason, with the cap kept for the tail and reported as a halt, so a partial review is never presented as finished.

quiz.stem: A market-research coordinator spawns four parallel subagents, one each for analyst reports, regulatory filings, earnings-call transcripts, and social sentiment. Each returns a solid, well-cited summary of its own lane, and runs are fast. Clients complain that the final report never connects a regulatory change to the sentiment shift that followed it. What should the architect change?
options: Give each subagent a larger context window so it can also hold material from the other three sources.
Let the four subagents exchange findings directly with each other so they can spot cross-source links.
Give every subagent access to all four source tools so each one can research the full picture itself.
Add an explicit synthesis step, such as a cross-source subagent, whose job is finding intersections.
quiz.explanation: The four lanes are genuinely independent, so the parallel fan-out is correct; what is missing is any stage responsible for cross-domain synthesis. Siloed output from a multi-agent system usually signals a missing aggregation step, not a model or context configuration problem. Adding that step keeps the parallelism and supplies the intersections.

quiz.stem: An on-call assistant reads an arbitrary production alert, decides which of about forty diagnostics to run, and picks each next diagnostic based on what the previous one returned. A platform lead proposes replacing it with a fixed pipeline that runs a standard set of diagnostics in a set order, citing predictability and cost. The surrounding steps of opening a ticket, attaching output, and paging the owner never vary. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Replace the whole assistant with the fixed pipeline, running every diagnostic in the same order for every alert.
Make the fixed steps a deterministic pipeline and keep a bounded agent loop only for the diagnosis stage.
Build a coordinator that runs all forty diagnostics as parallel subagents and summarizes what they return.
Keep one agent loop for the entire workflow, including ticketing and paging, with a higher turn cap.
quiz.explanation: The deciding test is whether the next step depends on the content of the previous result. Diagnosis does, so it needs an agent; ticketing, attaching, and paging do not, so they belong in code where they are predictable and cannot be skipped. A narrow, bounded agent inside one stage of a deterministic pipeline gets both properties.

quiz.stem: A code-modernization coordinator analyzes three independent modules before planning, and each analysis takes about four minutes. The analysis phase takes about twelve minutes end to end, and transcripts show the coordinator issuing one subagent call, waiting for its result, then issuing the next. No module analysis uses another module's findings. Which change most directly cuts the latency?
options: Have the coordinator emit all three subagent calls in a single response so the analyses run concurrently.
Switch the module-analysis subagents to a smaller model so each of the three analyses finishes faster.
Raise the concurrent-subagent limit, because its default is keeping more than one subagent from running.
Merge the three analyses into one subagent so the coordinator only has to wait on a single delegation.
quiz.explanation: When no branch needs another branch's findings, the branches are independent and total time should be the slowest branch, not the sum. Issuing one delegation per coordinator turn serializes them; emitting multiple delegation calls in one response lets them run in parallel. A roughly threefold latency is the signature of this sequential anti-pattern.

quiz.stem: A research coordinator on an Opus-class model delegates readily, and a recent run grew into a tree three layers deep that cost several times its estimate. The architect must bound total spend for the run, including everything the subagents spend, and stop workers from spawning their own workers, while the coordinator keeps delegating. Which two settings meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Set maxBudgetUsd on the coordinator's query, since subagent requests count toward the run's total cost.
Set maxTurns on each subagent definition, which caps the dollar spend of every branch in the tree.
Remove Agent from the coordinator's allowedTools so that no delegation can happen anywhere in the run.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 1 so that workers cannot delegate below the first layer.
Add a sentence to the coordinator's prompt saying subagents must never create subagents of their own.
quiz.explanation: maxBudgetUsd bounds the whole tree because subagent requests count toward total_cost_usd, and at the cap the query refuses new subagents. A spawn depth of 1 lets the main agent delegate while its workers cannot delegate further, which removes the nested layers. Per-agent turn caps and prompt sentences bound neither money nor structure.

quiz.stem: In a research system, the coordinator routes every web-search subagent's findings to a report-writer subagent. To shave latency, an engineer proposes letting the search subagents send their findings straight to the report writer. The compliance team requires a complete record of what each worker received and produced, and one place where failures are detected and handled. What should the architect decide?
options: Approve direct routing, and have each subagent log its own messages so the record can be rebuilt later.
Approve direct routing only for search subagents that return high-confidence findings, and route the rest centrally.
Keep all communication routed through the coordinator, which gives central observability and error handling.
Merge the search and report-writing roles into one subagent so there is no handoff left to observe.
quiz.explanation: In the hub-and-spoke pattern subagents never talk to each other directly; everything passes through the coordinator, which is what makes the system observable and gives failures one place to be detected and routed. The compliance constraint makes that non-negotiable, and the latency saved by bypassing the hub is small next to what is lost.

quiz.stem: A due-diligence coordinator runs three researcher subagents under a max_budget_usd cap. On a run that hits the cap, the coordinator publishes a report built from the two researchers that finished and labels it complete; the third researcher had been stopped mid-work. Analysts later act on the report without knowing a third of the sources were never covered. What should the architect change first?
options: Raise max_budget_usd so that all three researchers reliably finish before the cap is ever reached.
Remove the budget cap and rely on each researcher's maxTurns setting to bound the run instead.
Tell the coordinator in its prompt to mention any missing sources in the report's introduction.
Check the result subtype, treat error_max_budget_usd as incomplete, and name the uncovered source.
quiz.explanation: At the cap the query stops background subagents and ends with the error_max_budget_usd subtype, so a budget stop is an incomplete result, not a partial success. The wrapper must check the subtype before trusting the result and carry the coverage gap, two of three sources with the third named, into the human-facing output. Raising the cap only makes the failure rarer.

quiz.stem: A support coordinator has three subagents: billing-disputes, shipping-status, and account-security. Each has a detailed prompt and the right tools, but all three descriptions read "Helps customers resolve their issues." In testing, about a third of shipping questions are delegated to billing-disputes. What is the best fix?
options: Add routing rules to the coordinator's system prompt, such as "send tracking questions to shipping-status".
Rewrite each subagent's description as a routing rule stating when to use it and what it does not handle.
Give all three subagents the full set of tools so that a misrouted question can still be answered.
Move the coordinator to a larger model so it can infer each subagent's purpose from its name alone.
quiz.explanation: A subagent's description is the selection signal Claude matches tasks against, so three identical descriptions leave the coordinator guessing. Writing each description as a routing rule, with when to use it and what is out of scope, fixes the defect where it lives. Patching around it in the coordinator's prompt leaves the defect in place and competes with everything else in the window.

quiz.stem: In a Claude Code session, the main agent spends twenty minutes running a slow integration suite and isolates one failing test, its assertion error, and the cause: a timezone default in a date helper. It then delegates with the prompt "Fix the failing test we found; use the fix we agreed on." The subagent reruns the full suite, changes the test's expected value instead of the helper, and takes eighteen turns. Which change fixes the root cause?
options: Rewrite the delegation as a work order with the test, repro, error text, locked decision, and return shape.
Raise the subagent's maxTurns and switch it to a larger model so it can reason its way to the intended fix.
Add the timezone decision to the project CLAUDE.md so that every future agent in the repository applies it.
Give the subagent the Agent tool so it can delegate the slow suite run and stay focused on the fix itself.
quiz.explanation: A subagent's context starts fresh, and the only thing that crosses from parent to child is the delegation prompt string, so "we" and "the fix we agreed on" refer to nothing it can see. Rerunning the suite and editing the test are direct consequences of missing inputs. A self-contained work order carries the paths, failure text, locked decision, scope, and expected return.

quiz.stem: A regulatory research system has search subagents that each summarize ten sources into a paragraph of prose before handing it to a synthesis subagent. The final briefings read well, but auditors must be able to trace every claim to its source and retrieval date, and currently almost none can be traced. Which change best meets the audit requirement?
options: Instruct the synthesis subagent to cite its sources carefully and include retrieval dates in its briefings.
Pass the full text of every retrieved source to the synthesis subagent so it can cite from the originals.
Return findings as structured objects with source metadata and claim-source IDs the synthesis schema keeps.
Have the search subagents write longer summaries so that more of the source detail survives into synthesis.
quiz.explanation: Summarizing into prose silently drops attribution: once ten sources become one paragraph, no downstream agent can recover which claim came from where. Structured finding objects keep content separate from metadata such as source URL, retrieval time, and confidence, and the claim-to-source mapping via shared IDs must survive into the synthesis output, or the provenance chain breaks there.

quiz.stem: Two researcher subagents in a pricing study report different list prices for the same competitor product: one from a vendor datasheet dated March, one from a reseller page retrieved last week. The synthesis subagent currently keeps the newer figure and drops the other without comment. The client has said pricing conflicts must be visible to a human reviewer. What should the synthesis stage do?
options: Keep the figure from whichever source has the higher confidence rating and note that rating in the report.
Average the two figures and flag the result as an estimate so the reviewer knows it is only approximate.
Re-run both researchers until their figures agree, then report the agreed figure as the final finding.
Record a conflict object with both claims and sources, mark it unresolved, and escalate to the coordinator.
quiz.explanation: A subagent must never silently pick one of two conflicting claims, because that destroys provenance and hides a decision the client wants a human to make. The correct output annotates both claims with their sources, marks the conflict unresolved, and routes it to the coordinator, which surfaces it to the reviewer.

quiz.stem: A platform team puts its code-review standards in the coordinator's system prompt. The coordinator follows them, but the three reviewer subagents it spawns ignore them. The standards apply to every subagent on every run, and the team does not want compliance to depend on the coordinator remembering to restate them. Project setting sources are enabled. Where should the standards live?
options: In the coordinator's system prompt, moved to the top and repeated at the end for added emphasis.
In the project CLAUDE.md, which subagents load, or in each reviewer's own definition prompt.
In the coordinator's conversation history, which subagents read through the parent tool-use link.
In every delegation prompt, with the coordinator told to paste the standards in each time it delegates.
quiz.explanation: Subagents do not receive the parent's system prompt or conversation history. They do receive their own system prompt and the project CLAUDE.md through setting sources, so durable, universal standards belong there. That removes the dependency on the coordinator reproducing them on every call.

quiz.stem: A support system's policy-lookup subagent is meant only to read refund policy and order records. It currently inherits every tool, and last week it issued a refund on its own. The security lead wants it to be impossible for this subagent to call refunds_issue, while the main agent keeps that tool. Which change meets the requirement?
options: Set the subagent's tools list to only the read tools it needs, so refunds_issue is not in its session.
List refunds_issue under allowed-tools in a skill's frontmatter, with a note marking it as forbidden.
Mark the lookup tools with readOnlyHint so the subagent is limited to read-only operations.
Add a line to the subagent's prompt stating that it must never issue refunds under any circumstances.
quiz.explanation: A subagent's tools field is an availability list: a tool left out is not in that agent's session at all, so the action cannot be taken whatever the model decides. That is structural enforcement, the first rung of the enforcement ladder, and it leaves the main agent's tools untouched.

quiz.stem: An account-security agent can call verify_identity and reset_password. Despite clear system-prompt instructions, audit logs show roughly one reset in two hundred happening before identity was verified. Compliance requires zero exceptions, and when a reset is blocked the agent should explain why and escalate rather than retry. Which design meets both requirements?
options: A PostToolUse hook on reset_password that flags any reset made without verification for human review.
Moving the ordering rule into project CLAUDE.md so it is re-injected every request and survives compaction.
A PreToolUse hook that denies reset_password, with a reason, unless verify_identity has succeeded.
Several few-shot examples in the system prompt showing verification always happening before a reset.
quiz.explanation: A prerequisite gate is a PreToolUse hook that tracks session state and blocks the downstream tool until the upstream tool has succeeded. It runs in code before the call executes, so the model cannot bypass it, and a denial carrying a permissionDecisionReason gives the model the context to escalate instead of retrying with different parameters.

quiz.stem: A two-stage pipeline extracts claims data to a staging file and then loads it into a warehouse. The load stage starts whenever a handoff file exists in the run folder. After a crash and rerun, the loader picked up a handoff left by the earlier aborted run and loaded a stale, half-validated dataset. What is the most robust fix at the stage boundary?
options: Have the extraction stage write a more detailed prose summary of what it validated for the loader to read.
Include the extracted dataset inline in the handoff so the loader never reads a stale file from storage.
Have the load agent message the extraction agent to confirm the run is current before it starts loading.
Have the loader validate run id, expected next stage, a code-evaluated gate status, and the checksum first.
quiz.explanation: A handoff record makes a stage boundary real only if the next stage validates it before acting. Refusing on a run or stage mismatch, a gate status other than pass, or a checksum that does not match the artifact turns stale or out-of-order work into a loud failure at the boundary. That refusal is the enforcement.

quiz.stem: A long-running Claude Code job in CI migrates a large codebase. The opening prompt says never to edit files under db/migrations/applied/. The conversation compacts twice, and afterward the agent edits an applied migration. The team wants the rule enforced every time and still visible to the model after compaction, so it plans around the rule. Which two changes should they make? (Select TWO.)
options: Repeat the rule three times in the opening prompt so that at least one copy survives each compaction.
Add a PreToolUse hook that denies Edit and Write on paths under db/migrations/applied/ with a reason.
Raise the compaction trigger so that the opening prompt is summarized away later in the run.
Move the rule into the project CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected into context on every request.
Mark the applied migration files with readOnlyHint so the agent's tools treat them as read-only.
quiz.explanation: Instructions in an opening prompt can be dropped when a long conversation compacts. A PreToolUse deny enforces the rule deterministically whatever the model remembers, and CLAUDE.md, re-injected on every request, keeps the rule in view so the model plans around it instead of repeatedly colliding with the hook. Enforcement and visibility are separate jobs.

quiz.stem: When the refund agent escalates, it writes a friendly paragraph to the human queue. Human agents report opening the full conversation transcript for almost every ticket to find the order, what was tried, and why it failed, which doubles handling time. Which change best reduces handling time?
options: Attach the full conversation transcript to each ticket so the human agent has everything in one place.
Emit a structured handoff: customer id, issue, root cause, attempts, escalation reason, amount, next step.
Instruct the agent to write a longer, more detailed escalation paragraph that covers the whole conversation.
Let human agents resume the agent's session so they can question it about the case directly.
quiz.explanation: A handoff to a human should be self-contained: the person acting on it should never need the transcript. Structured fields for the verified customer, the problem, what was attempted and why it failed, the specific policy that required escalation, and a recommended action put exactly the decision inputs in front of the reviewer.

quiz.stem: A multi-stage financial extraction pipeline hands work between subagents. Stage one agreed with the client to store all amounts in minor units and all dates in UTC. Stage three, running later from its own work order, stored amounts in major units, and reconciled totals were off by a factor of one hundred. The handoff between stages carries only artifact paths. What should the architect add?
options: A decisions_locked field in the handoff record that the next stage reads and must not relitigate.
Stage one's full conversation history, passed to stage three so it can see how the decision was made.
A line in stage three's prompt telling it to stay consistent with whatever earlier stages decided.
A larger model for stage three so that it infers the unit convention from the data it receives.
quiz.explanation: Settled decisions have to travel with the work, or the next stage rediscovers them differently, which is the most expensive form of subagent drift. A decisions_locked list in the handoff record makes the convention explicit, and because the next stage validates the record before acting, the decision is carried by contract rather than hope.

quiz.stem: A support agent's order tool returns raw fields: ordered_at as an epoch integer, status as a numeric code, amount_cents, and tier codes such as P1. The agent sometimes quotes the wrong order date or calls a delivered order "processing". The tool is owned by another team and cannot be changed. Which fix removes these misreadings most reliably?
options: Document every status code, tier code, and the epoch format in the system prompt so the model can decode them.
Add a PreToolUse hook on the order tool that rewrites the order id into the format the API expects.
Add a PostToolUse hook that converts the raw fields into plain values before the model sees them.
Add a separate decode_order tool that the agent can call to translate raw fields whenever it is unsure.
quiz.explanation: PostToolUse runs after the tool returns and before the model sees the result, which makes it the normalization window. Converting raw fields there, and even embedding business meaning such as what a tier entitles the customer to, removes interpretation surface: the model cannot misread what it never sees raw. It needs no change to the other team's tool and no extra tool call.

quiz.stem: A CI agent has two PreToolUse hooks matched to Bash. A normalization hook rewrites commands to use absolute paths and returns allow with updatedInput. A security hook returns deny for any command touching production credentials. An engineer worries that if the normalization hook runs last, its allow will override the security hook's deny. What change, if any, is needed to guarantee the deny always wins?
options: Register the security hook after the normalization hook so that its decision is the final one applied.
Merge both hooks into a single callback so there is one decision and no ordering question to resolve.
Make the normalization hook async so that it cannot interfere with the security hook's decision.
No change is needed for precedence, because deny beats defer, ask, and allow when several hooks apply.
quiz.explanation: When several hooks or rules apply to one call, the decision precedence is deny, then defer, then ask, then allow. The security hook's deny therefore wins regardless of registration order. Reordering or merging adds maintenance cost without changing the outcome, and making the normalization hook async would silently break it.

quiz.stem: A debugging assistant's log_search tool returns about 40,000 tokens per call, and after four or five searches the context compacts and the assistant loses track of which request ids it was chasing. It only needs matching lines with timestamps and request ids, but engineers occasionally need the full output afterwards. Which change is best?
options: Add an async PostToolUse hook that trims the output in the background so the agent is never slowed down.
Add a PostToolUse hook returning updatedToolOutput with just matching lines, plus a path to the raw output.
Add a PreCompact hook that archives the transcript so the raw log output survives when compaction runs.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the assistant to ignore irrelevant lines in log search results.
quiz.explanation: PostToolUse can replace a tool's output with updatedToolOutput before Claude ever sees it, which is where a 40,000-token payload becomes the few lines the agent needs. Saving the raw output and returning its path keeps the trimming reversible. The hook runs synchronously in your process, costs no tokens, and prevents the context pressure instead of recording it.

quiz.stem: An engineering organization wants two new agent workloads. The first reviews every merged pull request nightly against a fixed twelve-item compliance checklist, and auditors require the same steps in the same order each time. The second investigates intermittent production data corruption whose origin is unknown and may lie in any of several services. Which decomposition strategy fits each workload?
options: Prompt chaining for the compliance review, and dynamic decomposition for the corruption investigation.
Dynamic decomposition for the compliance review, and prompt chaining for the corruption investigation.
Prompt chaining for both, with the investigation's steps defined up front from the list of known services.
Dynamic decomposition for both, so that each workload can adapt its steps as it discovers new findings.
quiz.explanation: The deciding question is whether you know all the steps before you start. The compliance review does, and auditors need reproducibility, so a fixed chain of prompts is right. The investigation cannot define its steps up front because each finding decides where to look next, so it needs dynamic decomposition.

quiz.stem: A privacy review asks which code paths write customer personal data to application logs. The coordinator splits the repository across eight subagents by team-owned directory, and each reports only paths that begin and end inside its own directory. The combined answer misses most real leaks, because personal data is typically read in one team's module and logged by a shared logging module owned by another team. Which redesign best addresses this?
options: Split the repository into sixteen smaller directories so each subagent can trace its territory more closely.
Keep the eight directory subagents and add a synthesis subagent that merges their reports into one answer.
Decompose by question, such as one subagent tracing each log sink back to its inputs, not by directory.
Run the eight directory subagents sequentially so that each one can read the previous subagent's report.
quiz.explanation: The analysis is cross-cutting, so splitting it by territory produces partial answers and nobody positioned to see a flow that crosses a boundary. Decomposing by question lets a subagent follow the data wherever it goes. A synthesizer over the directory reports cannot recover flows that no subagent was ever asked to trace.

quiz.stem: A documentation tool uses a writer subagent and a reviewer subagent that pass an API guide back and forth until the reviewer approves. Each round trip includes the full draft and the reviewer's notes, costs have tripled over the past month as guides grew, and quality scores stop improving after the second round. Which change best addresses cost without hurting quality?
options: Add a third arbiter subagent that decides when the writer and reviewer have converged on a final draft.
Cap the exchange at three round trips so the writer and reviewer stop before costs grow any further.
Move the reviewer to a larger model so its notes are sharper and fewer rounds are needed in total.
Keep revision in one conversation, and delegate only independently checkable parts such as link checks.
quiz.explanation: Refine-and-recheck work should not be split across subagents, because every round trip rebuilds context the other side had a moment ago, so cost climbs while quality plateaus. Keeping refinement in one conversation removes that rebuild cost, and only the one-pass, independently verifiable pieces around it are worth delegating.

quiz.stem: A developer spent ninety minutes in a named Claude Code session building an analysis of a large service for a refactoring plan. Two days later they return to continue the same plan. In the meantime only two files changed, auth.py and stripe_handler.py, both edited by a colleague. Which approach keeps the prior work and avoids acting on stale results?
options: Resume the session and continue directly, since the agent will notice the changed files when it next reads them.
Resume the session and state which two files changed, telling it not to rely on earlier results for them.
Fork the session so that the updated files are handled in a separate branch from the original analysis.
Start a fresh session and redo the full analysis so that no stale tool results can influence the plan.
quiz.explanation: A resumed session restores what the agent knew, not what is now true, and the agent cannot detect external file changes on its own. When the context is still largely valid and the changes are few and known, resuming and explicitly declaring what changed triggers targeted re-analysis and keeps the expensive baseline. A fresh start is for when prior results are fundamentally stale.

quiz.stem: An architect has a session holding a costly two-hour exploration of a monolith and wants to compare two migration strategies, one serverless and one containerized, from that shared baseline. Both strategies will involve trial edits to files. They want the original session left intact and neither strategy's edits contaminating the other. Which two actions should they take? (Select TWO.)
options: Fork the baseline session once per strategy, so each gets a new session id with a copy of the history.
Resume the baseline session for the first strategy, then resume it again for the second strategy afterwards.
Give each fork its own working copy of the code, since forks branch the conversation but not the filesystem.
Start two fresh sessions and repeat the two-hour exploration in each so their histories are fully independent.
Rely on the fork itself to isolate file edits, since each forked session keeps a private copy of the repository.
quiz.explanation: Forking copies the history into a new session id and leaves the original untouched, which is the pattern for exploring alternatives from a shared, expensive baseline. But a fork branches the conversation, not the filesystem: edits made by one fork are real and visible to any session in the same directory, so the two strategies need separate working copies to avoid overwriting each other.

quiz.stem: A weekly security audit in CI resumes last week's Claude Code session to avoid the cost of re-reading the repository. This week a large restructuring moved or deleted hundreds of files, and the resumed agent confidently reports vulnerabilities at line numbers in files that no longer exist. The team still wants to benefit from last week's findings. What should the pipeline do?
options: Start a fresh session and inject last week's findings as a structured summary framed as hypotheses.
Keep resuming last week's session, but prepend a note saying the repository has changed significantly.
Fork last week's session each week so the stale history is isolated from the new audit's findings.
Resume the session with a larger context window so the agent can re-read the whole repository on top of it.
quiz.explanation: When tool results are fundamentally stale because the codebase changed heavily, resuming is counterproductive: the agent acts on its transcript with full confidence. A fresh session with prior findings compressed into a structured summary, explicitly framed as hypotheses to validate rather than facts, keeps the value of last week's work without inheriting its outdated view of the files.

quiz.stem: A support agent has an order_status_get tool described as "Returns order status." Transcripts show that when customers ask where a parcel is, the agent calls order_status_get two or three times with rephrased arguments before giving up, even though carrier tracking lives in a separate shipment_tracking_get tool. Tracking is needed in about one conversation in ten, and the carrier API is slow and billed per call. Which change best reduces the redundant calls?
options: Merge the two tools into one order_status_get that always calls the carrier API and returns status plus tracking together.
Add a system prompt rule stating that tracking questions must be answered with shipment_tracking_get, not order_status_get.
Rewrite the description to list its return fields, say it excludes tracking and ETA, and point to shipment_tracking_get.
Set tool_choice to force shipment_tracking_get whenever the customer message contains the words parcel, tracking, or delivery.
quiz.explanation: The repeated calls come from a description that never says what the tool leaves out, so the agent keeps hoping the missing data will appear. Stating the return fields, the explicit exclusion, and the next tool fixes the defect where selection actually happens. Merging would put the slow, billed carrier call on the nine conversations in ten that never need it.

quiz.stem: An extraction pipeline uses one tool, submit_document_fields, with a doc_type enum of invoice or contract. line_items is required only when doc_type is invoice, and governing_law only when it is contract, so neither can be listed as required in the schema. About 12 percent of calls omit the field their document type needs and fail downstream validation. Which redesign best addresses the root cause?
options: Split it into record_invoice_fields and record_contract_fields, each marking its own type-specific fields required.
Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing which fields must be supplied for each possible value of doc_type.
Mark both line_items and governing_law as required on every call so that the schema rejects any omission at all.
Keep the single tool and add a downstream validator that re-queues any document missing its type-specific field for a retry.
quiz.explanation: A parameter that is required only when another parameter takes a specific value is the signal that one tool is doing two jobs. Splitting gives each document type a schema that can enforce its own required fields, so the omission fails at validation instead of downstream. Making both fields always required would push the model to invent a governing law for every invoice.

quiz.stem: A team built a custom MCP tool, code_semantic_search, described as "Tool to search through the codebase." For intent questions such as "where do we retry failed payments," the agent almost always uses the built-in Grep instead and misses logic that never uses the word retry. The team wants the agent to keep using Grep for exact-string lookups. What should they do first?
options: Remove Grep from the agent's tool set so that code_semantic_search is the only search capability it can select.
Add a routing subagent that classifies each question as exact or semantic and passes it to the matching search tool.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing intent questions routed to code_semantic_search and exact lookups to Grep.
Rewrite the description: finds code by intent, what it returns, when to prefer it over Grep, and not for exact strings.
quiz.explanation: Custom tools compete with built-in tools for selection, and a one-line description loses that competition because the model only has what was written. Enhancing the description with purpose, return shape, when to prefer it, and a negative boundary is the first and highest-leverage fix. Examples and routing layers come later, and removing Grep breaks the exact-match lookups the team wants to keep.

quiz.stem: A research agent has three tools: search_web ("Searches for information"), search_documents ("Searches documents for information"), and analyze_content. For questions about the company's internal policy corpus it alternates between search_web and search_documents almost at random, and web results sometimes contradict internal policy. The team has one week and wants the lowest-complexity fix that addresses the cause. What should the architect do first?
options: Move search_web into a public-research subagent and search_documents into an internal-research subagent under a coordinator.
Rename them search_public_web and search_internal_policies, and give each description its corpus and a pointer to the other.
Add a routing classifier in front of the agent that labels each question internal or external before any tool is offered.
Set tool_choice to any on research turns so the agent always calls one of the search tools instead of answering from memory.
quiz.explanation: The two descriptions are near-synonyms, so the model effectively picks whichever it reads first. Renaming with semantic weight and writing mutually exclusive boundary statements removes the overlap at the point of selection, which is the highest-leverage and lowest-complexity fix. Subagents and classifiers add architecture to solve a language problem.

quiz.stem: A CI pipeline gives its review agent one tool, manage_deployment, with an action parameter of plan, apply, or rollback. The review stage must run plan on every pull request but must never be able to change production, and the security team insists the guarantee cannot rest on the model following instructions. Which design best meets the requirement?
options: Keep manage_deployment and add a description sentence stating apply and rollback must never be called from the review stage.
Keep manage_deployment and add a PreToolUse hook in the review stage that denies any call whose action is apply or rollback.
Split into a read-only deployment_plan tool plus separate apply and rollback tools, and grant review only deployment_plan.
Keep manage_deployment and have the server declare readOnlyHint: true so the host treats review-stage calls as safe.
quiz.explanation: Plan and apply share a resource but carry very different risk, so they should not share one tool, one permission rule, and one audit entry type. Splitting on the destructive path lets the review agent simply not have apply, which is the top rung of the enforcement ladder: withhold the capability. A hook that inspects the action argument is deterministic and defensible, but it ranks below not granting the tool at all.

quiz.stem: A support agent's order_search tool returns an empty list both when a customer genuinely has no orders and when the order database times out. During a database incident the agent told dozens of customers that they had no orders and offered to open new accounts. The team wants outages handled correctly without retrying genuinely empty results. What should order_search return on a timeout?
options: The same empty list, plus a system prompt rule telling the agent to retry twice whenever order_search comes back empty before replying.
Return isError: true stating a transient timeout, retryable with a short retry hint, while real zero matches stay empty.
An uncaught exception, so that the agent pipeline stops immediately rather than acting on data that might be wrong.
A JSON-RPC protocol error, so that the client treats the timeout as a server fault rather than as a normal answer.
quiz.explanation: An empty list on failure is ambiguous: the agent cannot tell a timeout from a customer with no orders, so it confidently acts on a false negative. Returning the failure as a tool execution error with isError: true and a transient, retryable classification lets the agent retry within a bound and then report the outage, while genuine empty results stay unambiguous.

quiz.stem: A research subagent calls fetch_filing on a licensed financial database. For filings outside the organisation's subscription, the server returns isError: true with the text "Request failed, please try again." The subagent retries each such filing six times, exhausting its budget, and the provider's audit log flags hundreds of denied requests. Which change best fixes the behaviour?
options: Classify it as a non-retryable permission error that names the missing entitlement and tells the agent to stop.
Lower the subagent's retry cap from six attempts to two so that denied filings consume less budget before it moves on.
Return the denial as a JSON-RPC error so that the client stops the call instead of passing a message to the model.
Have the server silently leave unsubscribed filings out of its results so the subagent never sees a failure to retry.
quiz.explanation: A generic retry message makes a denial look transient, so the agent keeps retrying something that can never succeed. Classifying it as a permission error with retryable false and the required entitlement tells the agent to stop and escalate, and a failure classified non-retryable is never retried however much budget remains. The gap must still reach the coordinator rather than disappear.

quiz.stem: A team is reviewing how its refund-service MCP server reports failures. Most failures come back as results with isError: true, and a teammate asks which, if any, belong in the JSON-RPC protocol error channel instead. The team adopts the rule that anything a well-formed call reached and the server's logic decided belongs in the result. Which TWO failures should be returned as JSON-RPC protocol errors? (Select TWO.)
options: The upstream payments API returns a 503 while the refund is being processed.
The client invokes a tool name that the server has never registered.
The refund is rejected because the order shipped outside the 90-day window.
The request is so malformed that the server cannot parse it as a tool call.
The session's service account lacks write scope on the payments dataset.
quiz.explanation: Protocol errors are for requests that never made sense as a call, such as an unknown tool name or a malformed request. The other three reached the server's logic, which decided the outcome, so they are tool execution errors returned with isError: true and actionable prose. Routing them through the protocol channel would remove the text the model uses to recover.

quiz.stem: An extraction pipeline's orchestrator code must decide, for every failed document, whether to requeue it, send it to a person, or drop it. Today the MCP tools return failures as prose only, such as "Vendor master lookup timed out, try later," and the orchestrator parses that text with regular expressions that break whenever a message is reworded. The model's own recovery from these messages works well. Which change best fixes the orchestrator without hurting the model?
options: Standardise the wording of every error message in a shared template and keep the orchestrator's regular expressions.
Return every failure as a JSON-RPC error with a distinct numeric code that the orchestrator can switch on directly.
Replace the prose with a compact JSON code block only, since both the orchestrator and the model can read JSON.
Keep the prose in the content block and add error_class, retryable, and a retry hint in structuredContent.
quiz.explanation: The prose and the classification serve two different readers: the sentence is for the model, which reasons in language, and the machine-readable fields are for orchestration code, which needs something stable to branch on. Adding structuredContent alongside the unchanged prose gives the orchestrator reliable fields and preserves the model recovery that already works.

quiz.stem: In a multi-agent research system, a subagent's web fetch occasionally times out. Today the subagent returns the raw failure to the coordinator on the first timeout, and the coordinator aborts the whole research run, discarding findings the other subagents already returned. The timeouts usually clear within seconds. Which change best improves resilience?
options: Have the coordinator re-run every failed fetch itself, with backoff, so that all recovery logic lives in a single place.
Raise the subagent's turn cap so that it has more room to keep working after the timeout has occurred.
Retry transient failures locally in the subagent, bounded, and escalate a structured error only when retries run out.
Have the subagent return an empty result on timeout so that the coordinator can carry on with the other findings.
quiz.explanation: Subagents should handle their own transient failures and involve the coordinator only when local options are exhausted, and then with a structured error it can route on. Aborting the entire run on one failure is an all-or-nothing anti-pattern. The coordinator can then continue with partial results and report the gap instead of discarding everything.

quiz.stem: In a research system, the synthesis agent inherits every tool the coordinator has, including web_search and fetch_url. Instead of writing up the findings it was handed, it often launches new searches, which blows its budget and adds sources nobody verified. It still needs verify_fact to check claims against the collected sources. Which change best fixes this?
options: Set disallowedTools: web_search on the synthesis agent so the rest of its inherited tools, including verify_fact, stay available.
Give the synthesis agent a tools allowlist with verify_fact and what synthesis needs, and nothing that gathers new sources.
Set tool_choice to none on the synthesis agent's requests so it cannot start any new tool calls at all.
Add an instruction to the synthesis agent's prompt saying it must not perform new research under any circumstances.
quiz.explanation: Surgical scoping keeps the synthesis agent on the data already gathered: an allowlist closes its tool pool by construction, so research tools are simply not there. A denylist over an inherited pool fails by omission, because fetch_url and any tool added later still reach it. Blocking all tool calls would also block the verify_fact calls it genuinely needs.

quiz.stem: A document-intake pipeline registers three extraction tools, record_invoice, record_receipt, and record_purchase_order, and the document type is only known after the model reads the file. With tool_choice left on auto, about one response in ten is a prose summary instead of a tool call, which the ingestion step cannot parse. Which tool_choice setting best fixes this?
options: any, so the model must call one of the three extraction tools and chooses the one that matches the document type.
tool with name record_invoice, because invoices are the most common document type arriving in the intake queue.
auto, plus a prompt instruction telling the model that it must always respond by calling exactly one extraction tool.
none, with all three schemas pasted into the prompt so that the model writes matching JSON as plain text.
quiz.explanation: The requirement is that some structured result is always produced, and any of the three schemas is acceptable because the model has to pick the one that fits the document. any forces a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to the model, which eliminates text-only responses. Forcing one named tool is right only when a single schema is the deliverable.

quiz.stem: A team registers an incident-management MCP server with 45 tools in the project's shared configuration. Only the incident-triage subagent ever uses it, but every developer's main session now carries those 45 tool definitions, and the main agent's tool selection has become noticeably less accurate. Which change best targets the cause?
options: Turn on deferred tool loading so the 45 definitions are fetched through tool search only when the main agent needs one.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling the main agent to ignore every tool that comes from the incident server.
Move the server into each triage engineer's user-scope configuration so it stays out of everyone else's sessions.
Remove the server from the shared configuration and declare it in the incident-triage subagent's own mcpServers field.
quiz.explanation: Every registered tool costs context and adds a candidate to every selection decision, so the fix is to put the capability where it is used. Declaring the server inline in the one subagent that needs it moves both the tools and their description cost out of the parent conversation. Deferral reduces context cost but leaves the capability in the wrong agent.

quiz.stem: A customer support coordinator agent has 28 tools covering billing, orders, shipping, and outbound messages, and it picks the wrong tool on about one turn in six. Three of its tools, get_order_header, get_order_lines, and get_order_payments, are called in that order on nearly every order question. Which TWO changes most directly reduce misselection? (Select TWO.)
options: Set tool_choice to any on every turn so the coordinator always commits to a tool instead of hesitating.
Split the work into an order agent and a messaging agent, each with an allowlist of only its role's tools.
Raise the coordinator's maximum turn count so it has room to recover after picking the wrong tool.
Add a table to the system prompt mapping common customer intents to the exact tool names to call.
Consolidate the three order tools that are always called in sequence into a single order_details tool.
quiz.explanation: Consolidation removes candidates outright, and role-based distribution shrinks the set each agent chooses from; together they rank highest for reducing ambiguity. Forcing a call, raising the turn cap, or adding a prompt table all leave 28 near-neighbour candidates in front of a single agent.

quiz.stem: A developer connected a shared Postgres MCP server using claude mcp add with no scope flag, and it works well on their machine. Two new teammates who cloned the repository report that the database tools are simply not there. The team wants every contributor to get the same definition from version control without anyone's password being committed. What should the developer do?
options: Re-add the server with the user scope flag so it applies across all of the developer's projects, not just this one.
Commit their ~/.claude.json file to the repository so that teammates receive exactly the same configuration.
Define the server in a project-scoped .mcp.json at the repository root, referencing the password as ${DB_PASSWORD}.
Add a README section telling each teammate to run the same claude mcp add command on their own machine.
quiz.explanation: claude mcp add with no scope writes to local scope, which is private to that developer, so teammates never receive it. Project scope lives in .mcp.json at the repository root and is meant for version control, and ${VAR} expansion keeps the secret in each developer's environment instead of in the file.

quiz.stem: A committed .mcp.json passes an issue-tracker token as Bearer ${ISSUE_TOKEN} with no default, and it works on every developer laptop. In the CI job the server loads, claude mcp list prints a warning, and every call to the tracker fails with an authentication error. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
options: ISSUE_TOKEN is unset in CI, so the literal ${ISSUE_TOKEN} text is sent; inject the token from the CI secret store.
The headers field does not expand variables in CI; hard-code the token in a CI-only copy of the .mcp.json file.
The token needs a fallback so fresh environments work; change the value to ${ISSUE_TOKEN:-<shared service token>}.
Project servers need an interactive approval CI cannot give; add the server to disabledMcpjsonServers in CI.
quiz.explanation: When a referenced variable is unset and has no default, the configuration still loads, claude mcp list warns, and the literal placeholder is sent, which surfaces later as an authentication failure. The fix is to supply the secret in CI from its secret store; the missing default on the token is deliberate, so the file never carries a credential.

quiz.stem: An internal MCP server exposes run_release_checklist as a tool. Release managers want to start the checklist deliberately at a moment they choose, but the agent keeps invoking it on its own whenever a conversation mentions a release, which pages the on-call team. Which change best fits the capability to the right MCP primitive?
options: Keep it as a tool and add a description sentence saying to call it only when a release manager explicitly asks.
Expose it as an MCP prompt so a person selects it deliberately, for example as a slash command in Claude Code.
Expose it as an MCP resource so that the host application decides when to include the checklist in context.
Keep it as a tool and set tool_choice to none on every request so that the agent can never call it by itself.
quiz.explanation: Tools are model-controlled, so the model reaches for this one on its own judgment. Prompts are user-controlled and canonically invoked as slash commands, which matches a workflow a person must start deliberately. The capability sits in the wrong primitive, and wording or request-level blocks do not change who is in control.

quiz.stem: A team connects a third-party MCP server to its code-generation workflow. The server's export_repository tool declares readOnlyHint: true, but an export copies the entire repository to external storage. The team requires a person to confirm every export and wants only the release subagent able to export at all. Which TWO measures provide real enforcement? (Select TWO.)
options: Grant mcp__vendor__export_repository only in the release subagent's tools allowlist and in no other agent.
Trust the server's readOnlyHint and let the host skip its confirmation prompt for this tool automatically.
Write a permission rule against the exact tool name that requires a person to approve each export call.
Add a system prompt instruction telling every agent to ask the user before calling any export tool.
Ask the vendor to change the annotation to destructiveHint: true so the host starts showing confirmations.
quiz.explanation: Annotations are hints written by the server, and clients must treat them as untrusted, so neither the current hint nor a changed one is a boundary. Real enforcement comes from the tool set each agent is granted and from permission rules written against the exact mcp__server__tool name. A prompt instruction is a request, not a guarantee.

quiz.stem: A code-generation agent must replace every call to a deprecated legacyAuth() function in a monorepo of about 4,000 files. Its current approach globs every source file and reads each one in full before planning, and it runs out of context before touching the first call site. Which approach should the architect specify?
options: Read every file under src/ first so the agent has complete context before it plans any of the changes.
Run grep -r through Bash, save the output to a file, and then Read that whole file to plan the changes.
Glob for all TypeScript files, then Read each match in turn until all of the call sites have been found.
Grep for legacyAuth( to list the files, Read only the relevant regions, then Edit each call site.
quiz.explanation: The incremental pattern lets Grep say what to read: find the call sites by content, load only those files or regions, then make targeted edits. Bulk reading consumes the context window before any reasoning happens, and Glob matches names rather than contents, so it cannot locate call sites.

quiz.stem: An agent must change timeout: 30 to timeout: 60 in the payments handler of a 2,500-line configuration module. The Edit call fails because timeout: 30 appears seven times in the file, and only the payments handler should change. On earlier tasks, full-file rewrites of this module silently dropped unrelated blocks. What should the agent do?
options: Retry Edit with old_string widened to include the payments handler's surrounding lines so it matches exactly once.
Retry Edit with replace_all set to true so that every occurrence of timeout: 30 is updated in a single call.
Read the full module, then use Write to regenerate it with the new value placed only in the payments handler.
Use Bash to run sed with a regular expression that targets timeout: 30 across the whole file.
quiz.explanation: Edit requires old_string to match exactly once, so the fix is to widen the anchor with surrounding context until it is unique, which keeps the change surgical in a large file. Regenerating the module with Write reintroduces the dropped-code risk the stem describes, and replace_all or a file-wide sed would change handlers that must stay at 30.

quiz.stem: A CI job's agent must list every file named *.env.example in the repository, including files under a generated/ directory that is listed in .gitignore, and find every line in tracked source that mentions API_KEY. The security team wants permission rules that name capabilities precisely rather than match shell command strings. Which tool plan best meets both needs?
options: Use Grep for both tasks, since Grep can match file names as well as file contents across the repository.
Use Bash with find for the file list and grep -rn for the API_KEY lines, since the shell covers every directory.
Use Glob with **/*.env.example for the file list, and Grep for API_KEY in content mode for the source lines.
Use Glob for both tasks, first finding the files by name and then matching API_KEY with a second pattern.
quiz.explanation: Glob matches names and paths and ignores .gitignore by default, so it sees the generated/ directory; Grep searches contents and respects .gitignore, which suits tracked source. Both are narrow, read-only tools that a permission rule can name directly. Bash would find the files too, but it trades that precision for rules that must pattern-match command strings.

quiz.stem: A developer-productivity agent runs export DEPLOY_ENV=staging in one Bash call, then runs ./preflight.sh in the next Bash call. The script reports that it is checking production, its default when DEPLOY_ENV is unset. An earlier cd into the scripts/ directory did carry over between the same two calls. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
options: Bash output was truncated and hid an earlier error; raise the output limit and run the two commands again.
Each Bash call runs in a separate process, so the export is lost; set the variable in the same command as the script.
The working directory also reset between the calls, so the script ran from the wrong folder; use an absolute path.
Shell startup aliases and functions are not loaded in Claude Code, so export behaved differently; define the variable in an alias.
quiz.explanation: Claude Code runs each Bash command in a separate process: the working directory carries over within the project, but environment variables do not, so an export is gone by the next call. Setting the variable inline with the command, or chaining both in one call, keeps it in the same process.

quiz.stem: Your team maintains the repository for a Customer Support Resolution Agent. The lead engineer's Claude Code sessions consistently follow the team's conventions for the refund tool's error categories, but a contractor who cloned the repository last week finds Claude ignores them entirely. The conventions live in the lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. The fix must reach every contributor and the CI job without any per-machine setup. Which change best meets that constraint?
options: Ask the contractor to copy the lead's file into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and keep the two copies in sync.
Move the conventions into a CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root so they sit beside the code.
Move the conventions into the project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) and commit it.
Add an @import in the lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that points at a conventions file inside the repository.
quiz.explanation: User-scope CLAUDE.md lives in the home directory and is never pushed, so it works only for its owner; this is the classic 'teammate is not getting the conventions' bug, and the first thing to check is the config location. Project scope is the only option that version control distributes to every clone and every CI checkout. The 'no per-machine setup' constraint rules out anything that depends on each person's home directory or on a gitignored file.

quiz.stem: A developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md says 'Write commit messages as a single imperative sentence.' The repository's committed CLAUDE.md says 'Use Conventional Commits: type(scope): summary.' Claude follows the project format on some commits and the personal format on others. The developer wants the project rule to hold reliably in this repository without changing how their other repositories behave. Which change is best?
options: Delete the commit-format line from the user file, keeping user scope to preferences a project will not contradict.
Move the project rule into ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, which loads after ./CLAUDE.md and therefore overrides the user file.
Restate the project rule in capitals with a note saying that project instructions always override user instructions.
Copy the project rule into a CLAUDE.local.md so it appears twice in context and outweighs the user instruction.
quiz.explanation: All CLAUDE.md scopes are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other, so a direct contradiction resolves arbitrarily from turn to turn. The fix is to remove the conflict, not to out-rank it, and a commit-message format is a project decision that user scope should not assert. If the format must hold every time, a hook enforces it; prose never does.

quiz.stem: A platform team's root CLAUDE.md holds API patterns, testing conventions, and deployment rules, and Claude genuinely needs all of it in every session. The backend and QA teams keep colliding in merge conflicts when they edit the same file. They want each team to own its section in a separate file, and they accept that the total context loaded per session will stay the same. Which approach best fits?
options: Move each section into a .claude/rules/ file with paths frontmatter so each team edits its own rule file.
Split the sections into topic files and reference each one from the root CLAUDE.md with an @path import.
Move each section into a CLAUDE.md inside the directory where the owning team works most often.
Convert each section into a project skill so it loads on demand when Claude judges it relevant.
quiz.explanation: @import organizes but does not economize: imported files expand into context at launch, so the cost equals inlining. That is exactly what this team wants, because the content must be present in every session and the goal is ownership and fewer merge conflicts, not a smaller footprint. Every other option changes when the content loads, which breaks the 'needed in every session' constraint.

quiz.stem: A Multi-Agent Research System lives in a monorepo with packages/coordinator, packages/web-search-agent, and packages/synthesis-agent. Each package has a different owning team that wants to keep its conventions in a file right next to its own code and review changes to it in its own pull requests. When an engineer works only in the coordinator, the web-search conventions should not be in context. Which configuration best fits these constraints?
options: Put all three sections in the root CLAUDE.md under headings such as 'For packages/web-search-agent/:' so each applies only to its path.
Keep a short root CLAUDE.md and pull each package's conventions into it with an @import per package.
Create .claude/rules/ files at the repository root with a paths glob per package, maintained by a central team.
Add a CLAUDE.md inside each package directory, owned and edited by that package's team.
quiz.explanation: Per-directory CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules both give conditional loading, so the deciding constraint is ownership. The sources recommend a per-directory file when each package owner maintains a file beside the code they own, and a central path-scoped rule when a convention spans scattered paths. Root-level headings and imports fail the loading requirement outright.

quiz.stem: The project CLAUDE.md for a code-generation repository contains 'Never commit directly to main.' Claude complies early in sessions, but in long sessions it has twice committed to main anyway. The release manager says this rule must hold every single time, for every contributor. Which change best satisfies that requirement?
options: Move the rule to the first line of the project CLAUDE.md, in capitals, prefixed with 'CRITICAL'.
Enforce it with a PreToolUse hook that denies git commit and git push when the current branch is main.
Ask IT to place the rule in the managed policy CLAUDE.md so no individual can exclude or override it.
Move the rule into a .claude/rules/ file whose paths glob matches every file, so it reloads on each file read.
quiz.explanation: Every CLAUDE.md scope, managed policy included, and every rule file is advisory context; none of them can block an action. When a stem says 'must hold every time', apply the enforcement ladder: withhold the capability or deny it in code, and a PreToolUse hook is the deterministic deny. Rewording, relocating, or reloading the prose only makes violations rarer.

quiz.stem: An engineer built a /security-audit command in ~/.claude/commands/ that scans dependencies and opens tickets for findings. Teammates who try it get 'command not found'. The team wants it available to every contributor, reviewed in pull requests like other code, and never triggered by Claude on its own initiative, because it creates tickets. Which setup best meets all three requirements?
options: Keep it at ~/.claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with disable-model-invocation: true and share the file on the team wiki.
Commit it to .claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with user-invocable: false so only deliberate runs can happen.
Add the audit procedure to the project CLAUDE.md with an instruction to run it only when a user explicitly asks.
Commit it to .claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with disable-model-invocation: true set in the frontmatter.
quiz.explanation: Scope is distribution: anything under ~/.claude is personal, while the project's .claude directory travels with the repository and is reviewed like code. Because the procedure has side effects, disable-model-invocation: true is the right control, making the skill user-only. user-invocable: false is its tempting mirror and does the reverse.

quiz.stem: A research team has a skill, /evaluate-sources, whose body is a list of criteria for judging source credibility. Run inline, it floods the main conversation with dozens of file reads across 60 collected documents. They want the main session to receive only a findings table with file references, and they need that table back in the same turn. Which change best achieves this?
options: Add context: fork, agent: Explore, and background: false, and rewrite the body as a task: evaluate the documents in $ARGUMENTS and return a findings table.
Add context: fork and agent: Explore, and leave the body as the list of credibility criteria so the forked subagent applies them to whatever documents it finds.
Keep the skill inline and add allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob so the evaluation runs with read-only tools and keeps the main session lighter.
Keep the skill inline and add argument-hint: [folder] so every invocation is pointed at one specific folder of collected documents.
quiz.explanation: context: fork moves the exploration into an isolated subagent, so the main session receives only the result. Because that subagent's prompt is the skill content, with no conversation history, the body must be a self-contained task rather than a list of conventions. A forked skill runs in the background by default, so background: false is needed to get the table in the same turn.

quiz.stem: A support engineering team built a /triage-ticket skill for their Customer Support Resolution Agent repository. The frontmatter contains argument-hint: [ticket-id], and the body says 'Fetch ticket $ticket and classify it.' When an engineer runs /triage-ticket 48213, the literal text '$ticket' reaches Claude instead of the ID. What is the most direct fix?
options: Change the hint to argument-hint: [ticket-id] required so the value is validated and bound before the skill runs.
Add allowed-tools: Bash(curl *) so the skill has permission to fetch the ticket and resolve the placeholder.
Add arguments: ticket to the frontmatter so the first argument binds to the $ticket placeholder in the body.
Move the file to .claude/commands/triage-ticket.md, because command files bind named placeholders and skills do not.
quiz.explanation: argument-hint only supplies autocomplete text; binding a named placeholder is the separate arguments field, whose names map to argument positions in order. Adding arguments: ticket is the smallest change that fixes the symptom. The distractors confuse hinting, permission, and packaging with binding.

quiz.stem: An on-call team is writing a committed /incident-snapshot skill that runs kubectl get commands and summarizes pod health for the incident channel. Only a human may trigger it, and the kubectl get commands it needs should not stop for approval prompts during that invocation. Tool restrictions are already enforced separately through the team's permission settings, so the skill does not need to block anything. Which TWO frontmatter choices fit these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: user-invocable: false, so Claude cannot start the snapshot unless a person asks for it.
disable-model-invocation: true, so the skill runs only when a person types /incident-snapshot.
allowed-tools: Bash(kubectl*), which pre-approves kubectl get and blocks unlisted tools for the session.
argument-hint: [namespace], so an invocation without a namespace is rejected before any command runs.
allowed-tools: Bash(kubectl get *), which pre-approves those commands for the invoking turn only.
quiz.explanation: disable-model-invocation: true is the user-only switch; user-invocable: false is its mirror and does the opposite. Skill allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the invoking turn and restricts nothing, so the right expectation is a narrow prefix grant with no blocking effect. The space before the asterisk is load-bearing in permission rule syntax. Source conflict to know: the lesson 11 deck describes allowed-tools as restricting tools, while the study-kit notes (checked against current Claude Code docs) say it pre-approves and restricts nothing. If an exam item frames allowed-tools as a restriction, answer in the item's own terms.

quiz.stem: A code-generation monorepo has 14 packages, and test files (*.test.ts and *.spec.ts) are scattered through all of them, often beside the source files. The team wants strict test conventions, such as no any types and explicit return types in test helpers, to load only when Claude works on a test file and never during ordinary source edits. No team owns the test conventions per package. Which configuration best fits?
options: Add a CLAUDE.md to each of the 14 packages containing the shared test conventions.
Create .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.spec.ts"].
Add a 'For files matching **/*.test.ts' section containing the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md.
Put the conventions in docs/testing.md and reference it from the root CLAUDE.md as @docs/testing.md.
quiz.explanation: When the condition is a file type rather than a directory, .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter is purpose-built: globs such as **/*.test.ts match at any depth, and the rule loads only when Claude works with a matching file. Directory CLAUDE.md files cannot target file patterns, the root CLAUDE.md cannot be conditional, and @import is for modularity, not conditional activation.

quiz.stem: A Structured Data Extraction repository keeps invoice JSON Schemas under schemas/, organized into subfolders such as schemas/invoices/v2/. A rule at .claude/rules/schema-conventions.md has paths: ["schemas/*.json"]. While Claude edits schemas/invoices/v2/line-items.json, /memory does not list the rule and Claude ignores its conventions. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Path-scoped rules load only in sessions started from the directory that contains the matched files.
Rule files are discovered only when the root CLAUDE.md references them with an @import line.
The pattern's brace expansions exceed the expansion budget, so it is used unexpanded and matches nothing.
A single * matches within one directory level, so the glob covers only JSON files directly in schemas/.
quiz.explanation: In glob syntax a single * matches within one directory level while ** matches any number of directories, so schemas/*.json never matches a nested file. /memory not listing the rule while a nested file is open is consistent with that diagnosis. Changing the pattern to schemas/**/*.json fixes it without moving anything.

quiz.stem: A developer added .claude/rules/terraform.md with Terraform naming and module conventions, and no frontmatter. Since then, frontend engineers report Claude suggesting Terraform-style snake_case names in React components, and every session carries the Terraform text even when no infrastructure file is touched. All Terraform files live under infra/. Which change best fixes both problems?
options: Add frontmatter with paths: ["infra/**/*.tf"] to the existing rule file.
Move the file to ~/.claude/rules/terraform.md so it stops loading for the frontend team.
