Add a first line to the rule body: 'Apply these conventions only to Terraform files under infra/.'
Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md under a heading that reads 'Terraform files only'.
quiz.explanation: A rule under .claude/rules/ with no paths list loads unconditionally at launch, which causes both the context cost and the cross-contamination. Adding paths frontmatter turns it into a conditional rule that appears only when matching files are touched. Moving it to user scope removes it from the people who need it, and prose cannot scope itself.

quiz.stem: In the Customer Support Resolution Agent repository, a developer added .claude/rules/refund-tool.md with paths: ["tools/refund/**/*.py"]. They report that Claude still ignores the refund conventions while editing tools/refund/policy.py, and they want to fix it. What should they do first?
options: Copy the refund conventions into the root CLAUDE.md so they are always present in context.
Rewrite the rule with 'MANDATORY' headings in capitals so Claude weighs it more heavily.
Run /memory after Claude has read tools/refund/policy.py and check whether the rule is listed as loaded.
Convert the rule into a project skill with disable-model-invocation: true and invoke it before refund work.
quiz.explanation: The stem asks what to do first, and the first move is diagnosis: /memory shows which instruction files and rules are loaded in the session, and a file missing from that list is your problem. Path-scoped rules load when Claude reads a matching file, so check after that read has happened. Only once you know whether it loaded do you choose a fix.

quiz.stem: A production error log shows a stack trace pointing to an off-by-one error in the paginate() function in a single file; the fix is obvious and a regression test already reproduces the bug. The team needs the hotfix shipped within the hour. Which approach should the engineer take?
options: Enter plan mode first, because any change headed to production deserves a reviewed plan before edits.
Launch an Explore subagent to map every caller of paginate() across the codebase before editing.
Start with the interview pattern so Claude asks clarifying questions about pagination requirements.
Execute directly: fix paginate(), run the regression test, and show the passing test output.
quiz.explanation: Plan mode pays off when a wrong first attempt would cost more than the planning round trip: uncertain approach, several files, unfamiliar code, hard to reverse. A clear stack trace with an obvious single-file fix fails every one of those tests, and the one-hour deadline makes the extra round trip actively harmful. The regression test turns 'done' into evidence rather than assertion.

quiz.stem: An engineer who joined last week must move a Structured Data Extraction pipeline from 30 regex-based parser files to a schema-driven approach, and there are at least two credible designs. A wrong first attempt would touch every parser and be painful to unwind. Which workflow best fits?
options: Start in plan mode, let Claude read the parsers and propose a phased plan, edit it with Ctrl+G, then approve and implement.
Execute directly with acceptEdits across all 30 files, relying on git to revert everything if the approach proves wrong.
Start in plan mode and, since plan mode blocks edits, keep bypass permissions enabled to avoid prompts during implementation.
Fan out one claude -p run per parser file immediately, since each parser can be converted independently of the others.
quiz.explanation: Plan mode buys a chance to reject an approach before any file changes, which is worth its round trip when the approach is genuinely in question and the blast radius is large. Every trigger in the stem points there: unfamiliar code, competing designs, 30 files, costly failure. Editing the plan with Ctrl+G is the cheapest correction available before Claude acts.

quiz.stem: A team lead is setting up a new billing-integration repository. They want every contributor's sessions to start in plan mode by default, and they are also counting on plan mode to guarantee that nothing under migrations/ is ever edited without approval, including in sessions where some engineers enable bypass permissions. Which TWO actions are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Set permissions.defaultMode to "plan" in the committed .claude/settings.json.
Rely on plan mode for the migrations/ guarantee, since plan mode blocks edits in every permission mode.
Add 'Always start in plan mode' to the lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the behavior applies to the team.
Protect migrations/ with a permission deny rule or a PreToolUse hook instead of relying on plan mode.
Plan mode stops Claude from reading files, so write the plan from the lead's description of the code.
quiz.explanation: The default is a shareable setting, so it belongs in committed project settings. The guarantee is a separate requirement: plan mode is a workflow control whose blocks are not enforced where bypass permissions are available, so a must-not-happen edit needs a permission rule or a hook. Keeping those two jobs apart is the point of the question.

quiz.stem: An engineer asks Claude to 'write a function that normalizes invoice dates to ISO 8601.' Each attempt looks finished, but review keeps finding failures on inputs such as '03/04/25', '4 Mar 2025', and blank strings, and the engineer has become the only source of feedback. Which change will most reliably make the iterations converge?
options: Rewrite the request as a longer, more detailed prose description of every date format the business accepts today.
Give input and expected-output pairs, including ambiguous and blank cases, and have Claude run them as tests.
Ask Claude to review its own output carefully and confirm that it handles every edge case before finishing.
Split the work across three parallel sessions and keep whichever function looks the most robust.
quiz.explanation: Refinement converges when each iteration produces a signal Claude can read. Concrete input and output pairs define done in a testable form and capture edge cases you would otherwise catch in review, and running them as tests closes the loop. Without that, Claude stops when the work looks done and the human becomes the verification loop.

quiz.stem: Deep into a long session, an engineer has twice corrected Claude on the same issue: an internal CLI tool keeps swallowing a non-zero exit code. Both corrections produced plausible changes that did not fix it, and the context now holds three failed approaches. What should the engineer do next?
options: Give a third, more forceful correction that lists everything that went wrong in the two previous attempts.
Switch the same session into plan mode so Claude can reconsider the approach with all three attempts visible.
Clear the context and start again with a better prompt that states what was learned and names a failing test.
Raise the session's turn limit so Claude has more room to keep iterating until the fix finally lands.
quiz.explanation: The sources give an explicit stopping rule: after two failed corrections on the same issue, clearing context and writing a better prompt beats a third correction. The accumulated failed approaches are part of the problem, so anything that keeps them in the window keeps the problem. Naming a failing test gives the fresh attempt a signal it can check.

quiz.stem: A team runs Claude Code overnight on unattended refactoring tasks. Several mornings in a row the transcript ends with 'All tests pass,' yet running the suite shows failures. The project CLAUDE.md already says 'Run the full test suite before finishing.' The team needs a guarantee that no unattended run ends while the suite is red. Which change best provides it?
options: Strengthen the CLAUDE.md line to 'You MUST run the tests and MUST NOT finish until they pass.'
Add a Stop hook that runs the suite and blocks the turn from ending while any test is failing.
Require Claude to paste the final test output into its closing summary before it finishes each task.
Add a PostToolUse hook that logs every test command Claude runs so the team can review the log each morning.
quiz.explanation: A test gate can be escalated from a request in the prompt, to a session-long condition, to a Stop hook that blocks the turn until your script passes. 'Guarantee' and 'unattended' push the answer to the deterministic end of that ladder. Requiring pasted output is good practice but remains a request, and logging is not prevention.

quiz.stem: A GitHub Actions step runs claude "Review the failing tests and suggest fixes". On a developer laptop the command works, because the developer answers Claude's follow-up questions. In CI the job sits idle until the workflow timeout kills it. Which change fixes the root cause?
options: Add --ci-mode so Claude suppresses its clarifying questions whenever it detects a pipeline environment.
Invoke it as claude -p "Review the failing tests and suggest fixes" so it runs non-interactively.
Set the environment variable CLAUDE_HEADLESS=1 in the workflow step before invoking claude.
Add --batch so the review is queued and the step no longer waits on an interactive session.
quiz.explanation: Without -p, claude starts an interactive session; when Claude asks a clarifying question in CI, nobody answers and the job hangs until the timeout. -p (long form --print) is the non-interactive mode: one prompt, one response, a clean exit, and an exit code scripts can branch on. Plausible-sounding alternatives such as --ci-mode, --batch, or CLAUDE_HEADLESS are recurring fabricated distractors.

quiz.stem: A pipeline runs a Claude review with claude -p, and a later step blocks the merge if any finding is critical. That step greps the prose output for the word 'critical', and it has both blocked clean pull requests and passed a real critical bug that Claude described as 'severe'. The merge check must decide on a field the pipeline controls, not on phrasing. Which change best meets that requirement?
options: Instruct Claude to end every response with the exact line 'VERDICT: PASS' or 'VERDICT: FAIL', then grep for that line.
Grep case-insensitively for a maintained list of synonyms such as critical, severe, and blocker.
Submit the review through the Message Batches API instead, since it returns a structured result for each request.
Add --output-format json and --json-schema with a severity enum, then gate the step with jq -e on structured_output.
quiz.explanation: Default prose suits humans and is unreliable for machines. --output-format json with --json-schema puts schema-conforming output in the structured_output field, and jq -e turns a field into the gate, so the model's wording and confidence are never consulted. Batches are the wrong tool for anything blocking.

quiz.stem: A pull-request review job runs claude -p on every push to an open pull request. Each small follow-up commit triggers a full re-review, and Claude reposts the same comments it made on earlier pushes; developers have started muting the bot. The runners are ephemeral containers. Which change best stops the duplicates while still catching problems in new commits?
options: Fetch Claude's earlier PR comments with gh in a prior step and pass them into the fresh -p session, asking only for new issues.
Use claude -c -p to continue the previous review session so Claude remembers the comments it already posted on this pull request.
Run the review only on the first push to each pull request and skip the review on every later push to that pull request.
Tell Claude to report only critical findings so that far fewer comments are posted each time a new commit is pushed.
quiz.explanation: Each CI run is a fresh session with no memory of earlier reviews, so it re-reviews everything. The documented fix is the deduplication loop: fetch the previous PR comments, pass them into the fresh session's context, and ask for net-new comments only. That keeps fresh-session objectivity while ending notification fatigue.

quiz.stem: A conventions gate runs claude -p on a shared self-hosted runner. It must apply the repository's committed CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ conventions, must not execute any hooks from engineers' ~/.claude settings on that machine, and should see the pull request diff without being granted shell access. Which TWO changes meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Add --bare so the run skips auto-discovery of the hooks, skills, plugins, and MCP servers on the machine.
Add --permission-mode plan so that user-scope hooks are prevented from executing during the review.
Add --setting-sources project so project configuration loads while user and local configuration is skipped.
Add --allowedTools "Bash(git diff*)" so that Claude can fetch the diff itself under a narrowly scoped permission rule.
Compute the diff in an earlier step, pipe it to claude -p on standard input, and allow only Read, Grep, and Glob.
quiz.explanation: --setting-sources project and --bare solve different problems: the first keeps project configuration and drops personal configuration, while the second drops all auto-discovered configuration, CLAUDE.md included. Because this gate exists to apply the committed conventions, --setting-sources project is the fit. Piping the data in, rather than granting a shell to fetch it, is the least-privilege way to supply the diff.

quiz.stem: A pipeline job uses claude -p to generate unit tests for changed code, then continues the same session with claude -c -p to review those tests before they are committed. The review almost never flags anything, yet the generated tests routinely miss negative paths. The team wants a review that critiques rather than rationalizes. Which change is best?
options: Keep the continued session but instruct Claude to be highly critical and to list at least three weaknesses.
Increase --max-turns on the review step so Claude has more room to examine each generated test.
Run the review as a separate job in a fresh claude -p session, with test standards supplied by the project CLAUDE.md.
Add --output-format json to the review step so its findings can be parsed and acted on by the later pipeline steps.
quiz.explanation: A session that wrote the code retains the reasoning behind it and tends to review by rationalizing; a fresh session has no prior reasoning to defend. The CI architecture rule is separate jobs, separate sessions, with the project CLAUDE.md loading the shared test standards into each new session automatically. JSON output and turn limits address other problems.

quiz.stem: A CI step asks Claude to review each Terraform plan with the system prompt 'Be thorough and conservative.' It posts about 45 comments per pull request, almost all on tag naming and formatting the linter already accepts. Engineers stopped reading the comments within two weeks, and a plan that made a storage bucket public was merged. What is the most effective first change?
options: Change the instruction to 'Be more conservative and only raise the issues that truly matter to the team.'
Post only the findings whose self-reported confidence score is above 0.9, and suppress everything else.
Replace the instruction with named REPORT categories and named SKIP categories, one structured finding per issue.
Lower the sampling temperature so that the same plan always receives the same set of review comments.
quiz.explanation: The noise comes from missing rules, not from a weak model: 'thorough' and 'conservative' do not say where your line is, so the model draws its own. Named REPORT categories (public exposure, wildcard permissions, unencrypted storage) and named SKIP categories (tag naming, linter-approved formatting) turn judgment into a rulebook. The course names categorical criteria as the most effective first step for false positives, ahead of confidence filtering or softer wording.

quiz.stem: A support agent flags conversations for 'potential escalation risk' so supervisors can call the customer back. It flags 38 percent of conversations, supervisors have capacity for about 5 percent, and genuine cases get lost in the pile. Leadership also insists that cases the agent is genuinely unsure about must stay visible to supervisors, not be silently dropped. Which two changes best meet both goals? (Select TWO.)
options: Replace the phrase with tests that must all hold, such as repeat contact plus a missed promised fix, and list near misses not to flag.
Keep only the flags whose self-reported confidence is above 0.85, and quietly drop the rest so supervisors see fewer, stronger cases.
Instruct the agent to be conservative and thorough, and to flag only conversations that show genuine escalation risk.
Add a required needs_human_review outcome, separate from flag and no-flag, naming the test that could not be verified.
Set temperature to 0 so that the same conversation always receives exactly the same flag decision, making the supervisor queue predictable.
quiz.explanation: Precision this low means the criterion has no stated boundary, so the fix is a conjunctive test plus an exclusion list naming the common wrong flags. The second constraint, keeping uncertainty visible, is met by a required third outcome: needs_human_review turns an unsure guess into routed work in a queue supervisors can see. The other options either give no boundary or hide uncertainty behind a number.

quiz.stem: A CI review bot already uses categorical criteria. Its security and logic findings are precise, but its performance category has a false positive rate above 60 percent, and developers have started ignoring the whole bot. Rewriting the performance criteria properly will take several weeks, and the team must restore trust this sprint without losing the security signal. What should the architect do?
options: Disable only the performance category, note its re-enable date in the prompt, and leave the rest untouched.
Raise one global confidence threshold across every category until the performance false positives stop, then lower it once the rewrite ships.
Add 'be conservative about performance findings' to the prompt and keep the performance category fully active.
Keep every category active and ask developers to ignore performance comments until the criteria rewrite lands.
quiz.explanation: Trust collapse spreads across categories, so one noisy category drags down the precise ones. Turning off only the noisy category isolates the problem and lets trust recover while the real criteria rewrite happens, and writing the re-enable date into the prompt makes it a forcing function. Lowering thresholds across the board would sacrifice the security signal that is working.

quiz.stem: A research system's verification subagent is told to 'flag any claim in the draft report that may not be adequately supported by the retrieved sources.' It flags 58 percent of claims, and spot checks show most flagged claims are stated almost word for word in a retrieved source. Flags go to analysts whose review hours are limited. Which change best raises precision?
options: Run the verifier three times per draft and forward to analysts only the claims that all three independent runs agree are unsupported.
Add the rule 'only flag claims you are highly confident are unsupported by the sources' to the verifier prompt.
Lower the verifier's temperature to 0 so that its flag decisions become fully reproducible across repeated runs.
Define 'unsupported' as a test, require a quoted passage for each decision, and accept zero flags as valid.
quiz.explanation: 'May not be adequately supported' is satisfied by almost any claim, so the verifier picks a permissive boundary. A stated test (for example, no retrieved source contains a passage asserting the claim or its figures) plus a required quote grounds each decision in the text, so a supported claim cannot be flagged without the verifier contradicting its own evidence. Saying an empty flag list is valid removes the pressure to find something.

quiz.stem: A CI review step assigns CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM severity. The same bug class, a missing null check on an internal API response, comes back CRITICAL on some runs and HIGH on others. The prompt already contains about 800 words of severity definitions, and you have room for only a handful of examples. What should the architect do first?
options: Add one clear, well-annotated example per severity level, such as SQL injection as CRITICAL, so every level in the scale is illustrated.
Rerun a sample of diffs several times, find where severity flips, and add reasoning examples for those cases only.
Expand the prose definitions with sharper wording that separates 'severe' impact from 'significant' impact.
Set temperature to 0 so that the same diff always receives exactly the same severity rating on every run.
quiz.explanation: Inconsistency here is not a hallucination: the model understands the task but resolves an ambiguous boundary differently across runs. More prose adds surface area for ambiguity, so the fix is demonstration, and a small example budget should go to the fault lines, not the obvious cases. Running inputs repeatedly to find where output flips tells you exactly which boundary cases to demonstrate, with reasoning that shows how to decide.

quiz.stem: A refund-decision agent uses four few-shot examples, all taken from the most common ticket type and all ending in 'approve refund'. In production it approves 41 percent of refund requests, while a policy review of a labeled sample says about 15 percent qualify. Reviewers agree the written policy text itself is correct. Which change is most likely to bring the approval rate in line?
options: Add four more approval examples drawn from other ticket types, so the example set covers the full range of tickets the agent actually sees.
Append 'approve refunds less often than you currently do' to the policy text so the agent leans toward denial.
Move the example block after the customer's message so the policy text carries more weight than the examples.
Replace the set with disputed boundary cases, balanced between approve and deny, including one that routes to human review.
quiz.explanation: An example set where every outcome is 'approve' teaches a prior about frequency, and easy examples carry no boundary information. Rebalancing the outcomes, choosing cases reviewers actually argued about, including a near miss on each side, and demonstrating the abstention path teaches the boundary instead of a direction. The policy text is fine; the composition of the examples is the defect.

quiz.stem: A contract extractor uses few-shot examples that show only an input contract and the output JSON, all taken from contracts laid out as tables. On contracts written as dense prose, it fills renewal_term with values it infers from other clauses rather than a term the contract actually states. The team can afford only two or three examples in the prompt. Which change best fixes this?
options: Rewrite the examples to show the reasoning, stated versus inferred and why inferred means null, using both layouts.
Add six more input-to-output examples from table-style contracts, each showing the complete JSON output, so the extraction pattern is reinforced.
Add a regular-expression pattern to renewal_term so that only well-formed duration values can ever be emitted.
Add 'DO NOT GUESS VALUES' in capital letters at the top of the prompt, directly above the example block.
quiz.explanation: Output-only examples teach the model to ask 'which example does this look like?', which breaks when the document shape changes. Examples that show the derivation (found here, stated or inferred, so this value or null) teach the decision rule, which generalises across layouts. The course resolves exactly this extracted-versus-inferred drift with a couple of targeted reasoning examples, regardless of document shape.

quiz.stem: An internal tool classifies Jira tickets as bug, feature request, or tech debt. Accuracy is 88 percent, and nearly all errors fall on two boundaries (bug versus tech debt, and feature versus bug) where engineers disagreed until a house rule was written down. You are building a small example set for the prompt. Which two properties should the example set have? (Select TWO.)
options: One example per label, drawn from the highest-volume ticket types in the backlog, so the examples reflect what the tool sees most often.
Examples drawn from the disputed boundary cases, with the house rule stated in each example's reasoning.
Examples the model already classifies correctly, to reinforce the behavior that is working and avoid confusing it with edge cases.
Examples pasted inline between the instructions without delimiters, to save tokens.
Outcomes balanced across labels, with incidental features such as ticket length matched across labels.
quiz.explanation: Examples teach boundaries, and the errors sit on two boundaries the team itself found ambiguous, so the examples belong there with the house rule written into the reasoning. Examples also teach whatever else they share: a skewed outcome mix teaches a prior, and a surface difference like length teaches a length classifier. Volume and already-correct cases carry no boundary information.

quiz.stem: A shipping-document extractor asks for 'JSON only' in its prompt. About one response in 150 arrives wrapped in markdown code fences, with a friendly preamble, or with a renamed key, and the team's regular-expression repair layer keeps growing. The output is written straight into a system of record. Which change removes this whole class of failure?
options: Add 'RETURN RAW JSON ONLY. NO BACKTICKS. NO PREAMBLE.' in capital letters at the very end of the prompt.
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so that every reply is forced to begin as a JSON object.
Define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the contract, force the call with tool_choice, read its input.
Replace the regex layer with a tolerant JSON parser that strips code fences and maps renamed keys back.
quiz.explanation: Prompting for JSON yields JSON most of the time, and 'most of the time' is a parse error in production. Tool use with a forced call makes the schema a contract the API enforces, so fences, preambles, and drifting keys have nowhere to happen, and the result is read directly from the tool input. The other options either persuade, rely on a retired technique, or maintain repair logic forever.

quiz.stem: A support agent extracts fields from customer emails into a ticket through a forced tool call, and the schema declares order_number as a required string. When a customer never mentions an order, the agent fills in a plausible order number from the customer's recent history, and refunds are applied to the wrong order. The ticket system can already route tickets with a missing field to a person who asks the customer. Which schema change is best?
options: Remove order_number from the required list so the model can leave it out entirely whenever the email doesn't mention an order at all.
Type order_number as string-or-null, keep it required, and list every null field in a fields_not_found array.
Add a pattern matching the order-number format so that invented values are rejected at the schema level.
Add a retry that resends the same email whenever the extracted order_number fails the order lookup.
quiz.explanation: A required, non-nullable field leaves the model two choices, violate the schema or invent a value, and it invents. A null union kept in required forces the model to address the field while giving it a truthful way to say the email is silent, and fields_not_found makes absence an explicit, checkable act. The existing routing then handles the null tickets safely.

quiz.stem: A pipeline runs Claude Code headless on every pull request and parses the findings. The team passes --output-format json and expects the model's answer to match their findings schema, but the answer inside the result is often free text and the parser fails. Findings must conform to the schema on every run. What should they change?
options: Switch --output-format from json to stream-json so the findings arrive as a series of structured events.
Keep --output-format json and add a system-prompt rule telling Claude to answer only in the findings schema.
Add a tolerant parser step that extracts the first JSON object it can find anywhere in the result text.
Pass the findings schema with --json-schema and read the answer from the structured_output field.
quiz.explanation: --output-format selects the shape of the CLI's own wrapper document (text, json, or stream-json), not the shape of the model's answer. The flag that constrains the answer is --json-schema, and the conforming output lands in the structured_output field of the result. Confusing the two names is the classic trap here.

quiz.stem: A developer tool labels each pull request with a risk_level string. Most outputs are 'low', 'medium', or 'high', but occasionally it returns 'moderate-high' or 'med', and the downstream dashboard crashes on any unknown value. A colleague proposes adding "maxLength": 6 to the field. The team wants a guarantee, not a likelihood. What should the architect do?
options: Replace the free string with an enum of exactly 'low', 'medium', and 'high' in the schema.
Accept the colleague's proposal and add maxLength of 6 so long values like 'moderate-high' are rejected.
Add a field description saying the value must be one of low, medium, or high.
Add few-shot examples showing only the three allowed values in realistic pull requests.
quiz.explanation: The allowed values are enumerable, and enum is in the enforced slice of JSON Schema, so an unknown value becomes impossible. Length and numeric bounds such as maxLength are not enforced: the SDKs strip them, fold them into descriptions, and validate client-side afterwards, so they become a soft hint plus a post-hoc check. Descriptions and examples make the right value likely, not guaranteed.

quiz.stem: A synthesis subagent emits finding objects through a forced tool call, and a validator checks that every cited source_id exists in the set of retrieved sources. On failure, the coordinator appends the prior attempt and replies 'Validation failed. Please try again.' Second attempts fail the same way most of the time, and retries now account for a large share of token spend. Which change best fixes this?
options: Raise the retry cap so that more of the failing attempts eventually converge on citations that pass validation.
Drop the prior attempt from the conversation so that each retry starts from a clean and unbiased slate.
Return a tool_result with is_error true naming the finding, the bad source_id, the rule, and the next step.
Route every retry to a larger model, since repeated identical failures suggest the task exceeds its capability.
quiz.explanation: A generic 'try again' gives the model nothing to act on, so a systematic failure repeats while billing again. Appending the prior attempt and returning the concrete error as a tool_result with is_error true turns the next attempt into a correction task on known-bad output. Naming the field, the observed value, the rule, and the next action is what makes the feedback actionable.

quiz.stem: An invoice validator compares the stated total with the sum of the extracted line items, and on a mismatch tells the model 'total_amount does not equal the sum of line_items; fix it.' After this change the validation pass rate rose from 91 to 99 percent, but auditors now find invoices whose recorded total differs from the printed total, often with a discount line missing. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The reconciliation tolerance is too strict, so the model is rounding totals to force a match.
The feedback never said the printed total is authoritative, so the model overwrote it with its own sum.
The schema has no pattern on total_amount, so malformed numbers slipped past validation.
The retry cap is too low, so the model stops before it has re-read the document closely enough to find the missing discount line.
quiz.explanation: When feedback doesn't say which side of a discrepancy is authoritative, the easiest correction is to change the printed total to match the computed sum. That passes validation and destroys the evidence, turning a detected error into an undetectable one. The feedback should say the printed total stands and the model should re-check line items for a missed discount or credit.

quiz.stem: A warranty-claims agent extracts purchase_date from customer emails, and validation requires a date. For about 6 percent of emails the retry loop fails on every attempt, even with specific feedback such as 'purchase_date is missing; re-read the email for the purchase date.' Review shows these emails simply never state a purchase date. What is the correct architectural response?
options: Raise the retry cap for purchase_date failures, since specific feedback is already in place and should converge.
Strengthen the feedback to tell the model to estimate the purchase date from the order context.
Run three independent extraction instances on these emails and take the majority date.
Make purchase_date nullable but still required, stop retrying on null, and route those claims to a person.
quiz.explanation: Retries correct formatting; they cannot make absent information appear. When the data is genuinely not in the document, the loop will never converge, so the schema must allow an honest null while keeping the field required, and those records go to human review or a follow-up question. Retrying further, inferring, or voting all produce either cost or fabrication.

quiz.stem: An accounts-payable extraction pipeline has schema enforcement plus internal checks: totals reconcile with line items, and fields_not_found matches the null fields. Audits still find records that are fully self-consistent but were extracted from a delivery note or a quote rather than an invoice, and some name suppliers the company has never used. Which addition catches this class of error?
options: Check each extraction against your own reference data, such as the vendor master and issued purchase orders.
Tighten the schema with additionalProperties false on every object and stricter patterns on every field.
Add more internal cross-field checks, such as date plausibility and a second pass over line-item arithmetic.
Run two independent extraction instances and write only the records where both instances agree.
quiz.explanation: Validation has three tiers: structural (enforcement), internal semantic (does the record agree with itself), and external semantic (does it agree with the world). A coherent extraction of the wrong document passes the first two by construction. Only lookups against your own reference data, the vendor master and the purchase-order system, catch it.

quiz.stem: Every pull request triggers an AI review that must pass before merge, and reviews currently finish in a few minutes. Finance proposes moving these reviews to the Message Batches API for the 50 percent discount, pointing out that most batches finish within an hour. The team also runs a nightly full-repository security audit that nobody waits on. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move pull-request reviews to batch, since typical turnaround fits easily within the team's working day.
Move pull-request reviews to batch but poll every minute so finished results are picked up quickly.
Keep pre-merge reviews synchronous, since batch has no guaranteed delivery time, and move the nightly audit to batch.
Keep both workloads synchronous, since batch processing produces lower-quality reviews than the standard API.
quiz.explanation: Latency tolerance is the deciding axis. A pre-merge check blocks a developer, and batch offers no delivery guarantee within its 24-hour window, so it could block merges indefinitely. The nightly audit is the opposite case: nothing waits on it, so it earns the discount at no cost to anyone. When 'blocking workflow' meets 'batch', the answer is about timing, not quality.

quiz.stem: A nightly job has an agent explore each service repository through repeated file-read and search tool calls, deciding what to open next from what it has already read, and then write an architecture summary. Nobody reads the summaries until the next morning. Finance wants to move the job to the Message Batches API for the discount. How should the architect assess this?
options: Move it to batch as it is, because nothing waits on any individual result overnight and the 50 percent discount applies to every request.
Keep it on the standard API, because each run is a multi-turn tool loop that a batch request cannot service.
Move it to batch with streaming enabled so tool results can be fed back while the response is generated.
Split it into many small batches so each tool round trip completes and returns sooner.
quiz.explanation: Latency alone would favour batch here, which is what makes this tempting. But a batch request is a single turn: if the model asks to call a tool, nobody is listening to run it and send the result back, so an agentic exploration loop cannot run inside it. The second question in the batch decision is whether the task needs multi-turn tool calling, and here it does.

quiz.stem: A nightly job extracts fields from about 20,000 invoices through the Message Batches API. The loader waits for processing_status to reach ended, then writes every result it receives to the warehouse. Analysts report that 1 to 2 percent of invoices are missing after heavy nights, and nothing in the logs shows an error. What is the best fix?
options: Split the job into many smaller batches so that any single failure affects fewer invoices, and retry any smaller batch that reports problems.
Poll the batch status more frequently so results are collected before any of them can be lost.
Write a placeholder row with every field set to null for each invoice that is missing from the results.
Switch on each result type: load succeeded, re-queue errored or expired, and alarm on the failure rates.
quiz.explanation: ended means every request reached a terminal state, not that every request succeeded; errored, canceled, and expired are terminal too. A loader that treats ended as universal success silently drops that slice, which is why nothing shows in the logs. Handling all four result types, re-queueing the recoverable ones, and alarming on the rates turns missing data into a visible signal.

quiz.stem: A support organisation wants to cut model costs by moving suitable work to the Message Batches API. Some workloads face customers directly, some feed internal reports, and one uses an agent that looks up orders before deciding. Which two workloads are good fits for batch processing? (Select TWO.)
options: Drafting replies in live chat while the customer waits in the chat window.
Overnight re-tagging of last quarter's closed tickets against a new taxonomy.
Weekly quality scoring of chat transcripts, consumed by a Monday-morning report.
Routing each inbound ticket to the right queue under a two-minute service target.
A refund agent that calls order-lookup tools over several turns before deciding.
quiz.explanation: Batch fits when nothing waits on an individual result and each request is a single turn. The overnight re-tagging backfill and the weekly scoring job meet both conditions and earn the discount. Live chat and two-minute routing have someone waiting, and the multi-turn refund agent needs a tool loop batch cannot run.

quiz.stem: A developer uses Claude Code to implement a payment-retry feature, then, in the same session, asks it to 'review your changes carefully for bugs.' The review approves the change, and a race condition later surfaces in staging. The team wants reviews that reliably catch this kind of defect before merge. Which change best addresses this?
options: Have a separate instance, with no access to the writing session's history, review the diff.
Ask the same session to review a second time, this time 'as a skeptical senior engineer.'
Extend the same session's review prompt with 'double-check every line thoroughly before approving.'
Raise the writing session's reasoning effort so it thinks longer before it approves its own change.
quiz.explanation: An instance reviewing its own output keeps the conversation history and the reasoning it used to justify its choices, so it is unlikely to question them. A separate instance that sees only the output approaches the code with fresh eyes. The course signal is explicit: improving review quality means independent instances, not prompting the same instance to review more carefully.

quiz.stem: A single review instance reads entire 25-file pull requests in one pass. Its feedback is shallow, and it misses bugs where a changed function signature in one file breaks callers in another. Reviews run pre-merge and must finish within minutes. Which architecture best fits?
options: Keep one instance and add 'be thorough and check the cross-file impact of every change' to its review prompt.
Run per-file review passes in parallel, then an integration pass over their findings for cross-file issues.
Run five instances over the whole pull request and report only the issues a majority find, to filter out noise and false alarms.
Move the review to the Message Batches API so that each pull request can get a longer and deeper review.
quiz.explanation: Per-file passes give depth because each instance focuses on one file with clean context, and running them in parallel keeps the pre-merge review within minutes. A separate integration pass over their findings supplies breadth, catching dependency and signature mismatches across files. Vague instructions do not fix shallow feedback, and batch cannot sit behind a merge gate.

quiz.stem: A claims-document pipeline processes 300,000 documents a month with a single enforced-schema pass. About 5 percent of documents are hard: scans, handwriting, and unusual layouts. Leadership will fund at most about 1.5 times the current cost for additional review. Which trigger should decide which documents go to a verification pass?
options: A self-reported 0 to 100 confidence score from the extraction call, escalating any document scored below 80.
A random 5 percent sample of each day's documents, chosen to match the known rate of hard documents so review effort tracks real difficulty.
Validation failures, a confidence enum tied to handwriting or rotation, and scan quality, plus audits of unescalated ones.
Disagreement between three independent extraction instances that are run on every document in the corpus.
quiz.explanation: Tiered escalation (one cheap pass, verify only the flagged subset) lands near 1.2 to 1.5 times cost, inside the budget. The trigger should come from signals that need no second model call: tier-two and tier-three validation failures, a confidence field tied to observable document properties, and properties known before the call. Because the residual risk is triage recall, periodically sampling what was not escalated confirms the trigger is not missing a class of hard document.

quiz.stem: A research system classifies each source as primary or secondary by running three independent instances, and sends only disagreements to a human. An audit finds that a large share of unanimous 'primary' verdicts are wrong: news articles that re-report a company press release are consistently labeled primary. What should the architect change?
options: Increase to five independent instances so that a wrong majority becomes statistically less likely.
Add a verification pass that re-applies the same primary-source definition to every unanimous verdict and overturns any it cannot confirm.
Lower the temperature of all three instances so that their verdicts agree with one another even more consistently.
Rewrite the primary-source criterion with explicit tests, an exclusion for re-reported press material, and near misses.
quiz.explanation: Multi-instance agreement measures stability, not correctness. Every instance reads the same flawed definition, so they converge on the same wrong answer, and the unanimity reads as confidence. No review architecture fixes a bad criterion. The fix belongs upstream: explicit tests, an exclusion naming the common near miss, and examples on both sides of the boundary.

quiz.stem: A refund agent handles long chat sessions and uses progressive summarization to keep its context small. In one 45-turn session the customer first said the amount was $159.99, the order lookup tool returned $149.99, and the policy window stood at day 28 of 30. After two summarization passes the agent re-asked for the amount and then quoted $159.99. The team wants a fix that keeps context compact without depending on what the summarizer chooses to keep. Which change best addresses this?
options: Move to a model with a larger context window so the whole session fits and summarization never has to run.
Keep progressive summarization but instruct the summarizer to preserve every amount, date, and policy detail it judges important.
Keep a compact block of tool-confirmed facts (order ID, amount, policy-window day) pinned at the top of context, refreshed each turn.
Keep a compact block of facts updated from each customer message as it arrives, so the latest stated values stay pinned at the top of context.
quiz.explanation: Summarization that drops amounts, dates, and policy thresholds is a reliability bug, and identifiers and exact figures are the first things a model-written summary loses. Extracting transactional facts into a compact block at the top of context removes the dependency on the summarizer and also keeps them out of the low-attention middle. The block must hold verified tool data, which is what distinguishes the best answer from the near-miss that would pin the customer's wrong figure.

quiz.stem: A CI job runs a Claude agent that triages failing test suites. Each test-runner call returns about 20,000 tokens of log output, of which the agent needs only the failing test names, file paths, line numbers, and assertion messages. After five or six calls the agent starts attributing failures to the wrong test files. The team has a fixed per-run token budget and must keep the full logs available for later audit. Which change best fixes this?
options: Enable server-side tool-result clearing so the oldest log outputs are dropped from context automatically once a token threshold is passed.
Add a post-tool hook that keeps only failing test IDs, paths, and messages in context, saving each raw log as an artifact referenced by path.
Enable server-side compaction so the accumulated log output is summarized automatically into a short narrative once the session crosses the trigger.
Raise the maximum output tokens so the agent has more room to reason across all of the verbose log output it has collected during the run.
quiz.explanation: Untrimmed tool output is the dominant cause of context bloat, and the fix is to trim it before it accumulates rather than clean up afterward. Extracting the identifiers the next step needs keeps the context small and accurate, and recording the artifact path makes the trimming reversible, which satisfies the audit constraint. Clearing and compaction both act after the bloat and each loses identifiers in its own way.

quiz.stem: A developer has spent four hours in one Claude Code session investigating a flaky build tool. The investigation is finished and the work has moved to implementing a fix, but the history is full of abandoned hypotheses and the agent keeps reverting to an approach the developer ruled out two hours ago. The developer wants the implementation phase to start clean without losing two locked decisions and the exact file paths identified. What is the best move?
options: Keep working in the same session and add a strongly worded reminder that the ruled-out approach must not be used again.
Trigger compaction on the current session so the investigation history is summarized and the implementation work continues from that summary.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the earlier corrections stay visible alongside the rest of the history.
Start a fresh session with a handoff brief carrying the locked decisions, the ruled-out approach, and the exact file paths.
quiz.explanation: When the task has changed phase and the history is more contradiction than context, a fresh session with a handoff brief is the preservation strategy that fits. It has the highest one-off authoring cost and the cheapest steady state, and its risk is that anything not in the brief is gone, so the brief must carry the decisions, the exclusion, and the identifiers verbatim. Compaction would carry a model-chosen version of the contradictory narrative forward.

quiz.stem: A support agent escalates any ticket whose sentiment classifier score is strongly negative. The human queue is now overloaded with angry customers whose refunds were fully covered by policy, while a case where no playbook covered a partial refund on a bundled item was handled automatically with a guessed amount. The support lead wants fewer escalations and fewer unsafe automated actions. Which change best achieves both?
options: Escalate only on checkable triggers (an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or no progress) and resolve covered cases even if the customer is upset.
Raise the sentiment threshold so that only the most extreme negative messages escalate, and add a policy-gap check as a secondary escalation signal.
Add a self-assessed confidence score and escalate whenever the agent rates its own confidence below 7 out of 10, keeping the sentiment trigger as well.
Escalate any ticket that needs more than three tool lookups or more than two policy conditions, since complexity predicts where the agent is likely to fail.
quiz.explanation: Sentiment, complexity, and self-reported confidence are all unreliable proxies for whether a human is needed. The valid triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, and genuine inability to progress, each checkable against the record, and policy-covered cases should be resolved even when the customer is frustrated. That single change cuts the angry-but-covered volume and catches the uncovered bundle case.

quiz.stem: A customer writes 'Please refund my order, it arrived broken.' The account has two orders delivered this week, and the refund playbook requires an order ID; everything else the playbook needs is already present. The design goal is to resolve the ticket without guessing and without pushing extra work onto the customer. Which TWO behaviors should the agent's rules specify? (Select TWO.)
options: Refund the most recently delivered order, since it is the most likely match, and state the order ID in the confirmation message.
Ask one clarifying question that names both candidate orders and asks which one arrived broken, then re-evaluate the rules.
Escalate to a human immediately, because any ambiguity in the request means the agent is uncertain and should not act on it.
If the customer's reply is still ambiguous, route the ticket to a human instead of asking a second clarifying question.
Collect the order ID, damage photos, preferred refund method, and a reason code in one message before looking anything up.
quiz.explanation: When exactly one required field is missing and the customer can supply it, the right move is one clarifying question, then re-evaluation. The clarification budget is capped at one per ticket, and a second ambiguity escalates, because questions are cheap individually and corrosive in aggregate. Guessing risks a confident wrong refund, and escalating immediately is over-escalation.

quiz.stem: A damaged item bought in a clearance sale matches two playbooks: the warranty playbook says replace it, and the clearance playbook says final sale, store credit only. The current agent applies whichever playbook it matched first and sends the customer a confirmation. Leadership wants each such case handled safely and also wants to learn how often the policy itself is incomplete. What should the agent do?
options: Apply the playbook with the lower cost to the company, since conflicts should default to the most conservative financial outcome.
Ask the customer whether they would prefer a replacement or store credit, and then apply whichever playbook matches their answer.
Abstain: route it to the human queue as a policy_gap with both playbooks attached, and review that queue weekly to revise the policy.
Escalate to a human and, in the meantime, send the customer a reply saying the replacement has been approved and is now being arranged.
quiz.explanation: Two playbooks matching with conflicting actions is a policy gap, not a request ambiguity, so the correct path is abstention to a human with a policy_gap reason. Attaching the playbooks considered makes the case fast to decide, and reviewing that queue weekly is what reveals where the policy is incomplete, which is leadership's second goal. Guessing, or asking the customer to pick, hides the gap.

quiz.stem: A research coordinator fans out five search subagents. Two of them hit upstream timeouts, catch the exception, and return an empty findings list with status 'success'. The synthesis step then reports that no published evidence was found for the two subtopics those subagents covered. The team wants the smallest change that stops these false negatives while keeping the three good results. What is the best fix?
options: Instruct the synthesis agent to lower its stated confidence and add a caveat whenever a subtopic returns noticeably fewer findings than the others.
Have the coordinator discard the run and restart all five subagents from scratch whenever any subagent returns fewer results than expected.
Increase the subagent timeout and have each subagent keep retrying every failed search until it returns at least one result to the coordinator.
Have subagents return failures distinctly from empty results, with error class, retryability, and coverage counts, for the coordinator to act on.
quiz.explanation: The root cause is that a failure crossed the agent boundary looking identical to a genuine empty result, so the coordinator read 'not searched' as 'nothing found'. A structured return that separates what succeeded from what failed, classifies each failure, and carries coverage counts lets the coordinator keep the three good results, retry the transient failures within a bound, and propagate any remaining gap. Lowering confidence does not name the gap.

quiz.stem: A CI pipeline's coordinator delegates dependency, licence, and secrets scans to three subagents. Each subagent invented its own failure labels, such as ACCESS_PROBLEM, flaky, blocked, and denied_maybe, and the coordinator keeps retrying authorization failures while escalating simple timeouts. The MCP tools the subagents call already classify their own errors. Which change most directly fixes the misrouting?
options: Have subagents report error_class with the tool layer's transient, business, and permission values, putting situational detail in error_code.
Let each subagent keep its own descriptive labels, and add a translation table in the coordinator that maps every label to a retry decision.
Have subagents return a plain-language description of each failure and let the coordinator's model decide what to do based on the wording.
Collapse every failure into a single retryable boolean flag, and have the coordinator retry anything marked retryable up to three times before escalating.
quiz.explanation: Reusing the tool layer's taxonomy at the agent layer means the coordinator routes on one vocabulary and never translates: transient gets a bounded retry, business changes the plan, and permission escalates. The situational detail, such as auth_denied or upstream_timeout, belongs in error_code for the human. A second vocabulary only adds a translation step that drifts as new labels appear.

quiz.stem: A contract-extraction coordinator sends 40 contracts to extraction subagents. One subagent returns a well-formed partial result: 36 contracts extracted and 4 failed on unreadable scans, with a claim_scope stating those 4 were not examined. The coordinator's summary to the legal team reads 'No change-of-control clauses found across the 40 contracts.' Where is the defect, and what fixes it?
options: In the subagent: it should have kept retrying the four unreadable scans until extraction succeeded before returning any result.
In the coordinator: it absorbed the coverage gap; its summary must say 36 of 40, name the four contracts, and say why.
In the wording: the coordinator should add 'medium confidence' to its report whenever any subagent returns a partial status.
In the orchestration: the coordinator should re-extract all 40 contracts itself so it no longer depends on subagent coverage reports.
quiz.explanation: The subagent did its job; the gap disappeared one level up, when the coordinator turned 36 examined contracts into a claim about 40. Error propagation that stops one level short of the human is laundering, so the coordinator must carry coverage counts and the named gaps into the legal team's summary. Legal teams act on absence of findings, which makes this a reliability defect rather than a wording issue.

quiz.stem: Before a refactor, a developer asks Claude Code to find every call site of a deprecated chargeCard() function in a 3,000-file monorepo. The first attempt read the payments directory file by file and had used most of the context window before the refactor even started. The developer needs a complete list and a main session that still has room for the implementation. Which approach is best?
options: Read the payments and billing directories in full first, since most call sites are likely to live there, and then search the rest of the repository.
Rely on the large context window and load all of the repository's source files into the session at once so that no call site can possibly be missed.
Search for the symbol to get paths and line numbers, read only the matched ranges, and delegate the wide sweep to a subagent returning file:line hits.
List every source file in the repository, then read each one in turn and keep a running prose summary of anything that looks related to payments.
quiz.explanation: Exploration is a retrieval problem: a symbol search covers the whole corpus cheaply and returns a map of paths and line numbers, and only the matched ranges need to be read. Delegating the wide sweep to a subagent lets the exploration cost accrue in a context that is discarded, so the main session keeps its room for the refactor. The return contract of file:line identifiers is what makes the delegation worth paying for.

quiz.stem: An internal developer tool uses an exploration subagent, run as a forked-context skill, to answer 'why do some legacy endpoints skip authentication?'. The subagent returns 'Authentication looks mostly fine; a few legacy handlers might be worth a look.' The main session then re-reads the handler files itself, roughly doubling the cost of every investigation. Which change best fixes this?
options: Specify the subagent's return contract: exact files and line ranges, the bypass path, the test that would catch it, and what went unexamined.
Drop the subagent entirely and let the main session explore the handlers directly, since it ends up reading the same files anyway.
Keep the design, but have the main session always re-read every file the subagent read so that the subagent's conclusions are verified.
Run the subagent on a larger, more capable model so its summaries are more thorough and the main session can trust them without re-reading files.
quiz.explanation: The value of delegating exploration is entirely in what comes back: exact files, line ranges, and identifiers can stand in for tens of thousands of tokens, while 'looks mostly fine' spent the same money and bought nothing. Writing the return contract into the delegation removes the reason the main session re-reads. Dropping the subagent or re-reading everything throws away the context isolation that justified it.

quiz.stem: An engineer uses Claude Code to assess the blast radius of renaming a widely used config loader in a large service repository. The current prompt pastes the diff plus the full contents of every file that imports the loader, about 60 files, and then asks for a risk review. Reviews of large changes keep missing issues in files near the middle of the pasted material. Which change best improves reliability?
options: Keep pasting the full file contents, but place them after the question so that the most recent material sits closest to the actual request.
Split the 60 files into batches of ten, review each batch in its own session, and concatenate the six reports at the end.
Paste only the ten most recently modified importing files, since recent changes are where regressions most often appear.
Keep the diff and the importing paths in context, search for the loader's call patterns, and read only matched ranges and direct callers.
quiz.explanation: Pasting 60 whole files is an attempt to hold the corpus in the window instead of querying it, and material in the middle of a long input is used least reliably. Keeping lightweight identifiers in context and pulling matched ranges through search is just-in-time retrieval, and knowing which files reference a symbol says more about blast radius than reading any one of them in full. The other options rearrange, shrink, or split the same flawed approach.

quiz.stem: An invoice-extraction pipeline will auto-post any extraction whose self-reported confidence is 0.9 or higher. The threshold was chosen after a random 200-document evaluation showed 95 percent accuracy overall. Volume is 80 percent native PDF invoices, 15 percent scanned receipts, and 5 percent handwritten delivery notes, and finance allows at most a 2 percent error rate on auto-posted items. What should the architect do before go-live?
options: Go live at 0.9, since 95 percent overall accuracy on a random sample already shows that the pipeline performs well across the whole document mix.
Label a sample stratified by document type, measure accuracy per confidence bucket in each type, and set per-type thresholds to the 2 percent target.
Raise the global threshold to 0.97 so that only the extractions the model is most certain about are posted without any human review at all.
Ask the model to justify each confidence score in one sentence, and auto-post only the items whose justification cites specific extracted fields.
quiz.explanation: Stated confidence is a claim, not a measured probability, until it has been bucketed against outcomes on a labelled sample, and the mapping often differs by input type. A random 200 documents contains only about ten handwritten notes, so the aggregate figure can hide a failing segment while barely moving. Stratifying by document type and setting per-type thresholds against the stated 2 percent target turns the threshold into a decision instead of a guess.

quiz.stem: A claims-extraction pipeline has calibrated per-document-type thresholds, and only items below threshold go to human review. Reviewer capacity is fixed at about 10 percent of volume. A new insurer template starts arriving next quarter, and the team worries the thresholds will quietly go stale. Which addition best detects that drift without exceeding reviewer capacity?
options: Route every item to human review for the whole of next quarter so that any drift is caught directly on each item before it is posted.
Track the average stated confidence of auto-accepted items every week, and raise an alert if it drops below its historical baseline for any type.
Raise every threshold by a fixed safety margin as soon as the new template appears, so that more items fall into the human review queue.
Audit a stratified random sample of auto-accepted items per document type, oversampling the new template, and feed labels back into thresholds.
quiz.explanation: Thresholding gates individual items, but only sampling audits the population, including the items thresholding let through, which is the only way to see that a threshold has gone stale. A small stratified audit with the new template oversampled fits inside the fixed capacity, and feeding the labels back closes the loop. Confidently wrong items are exactly what a confidence-based monitor cannot see.

quiz.stem: A multi-agent research system is launching to draft regulatory-change briefings that compliance officers file with a regulator. It is brand new, and there is no labelled data on its accuracy. Leadership wants to save reviewer time by auto-approving any briefing on which three independent agent runs agree. What review design should the architect recommend for launch?
options: Review every briefing at launch, recording verdicts to build the labelled set later needed for calibration and sampling.
Auto-approve briefings on which all three runs agree, and send only the disagreements to compliance officers for review.
Auto-approve briefings whose synthesis agent reports a confidence of 0.8 or higher, and send the rest to compliance officers for review.
Review a 5 percent random sample of briefings each week, and let the remaining briefings be filed with the regulator without review.
quiz.explanation: Regulated output, a brand-new pipeline, and no labelled data are each on their own a reason to review everything. Recording verdicts during that phase builds the labelled set that later justifies calibrated thresholds and stratified sampling, which is how full review stops being permanent. Agreement among runs that share the same criteria is not evidence of correctness.

quiz.stem: A pipeline extracts figures from a company's annual report, two quarterly filings, and an analyst note into structured records, each carrying a source_id and page. A final merge step then writes a single company_profile paragraph for credit analysts. Analysts cannot tell which filing a revenue figure came from and end up re-reading all four documents. Which change best fixes this?
options: Append a bibliography of the four documents, with titles and dates, below the profile paragraph so analysts know what was consulted.
Instruct the merge step to write 'according to the filings' beside each figure, so readers know that every figure came from a source.
Have the merge step output claims and sources arrays linked by source_id, with a quote and page per claim, and render the prose from them.
Add an overall confidence rating to the profile paragraph so that analysts know how much weight to give to the figures it contains.
quiz.explanation: The provenance chain existed in the extracted records and broke at the merge step, because a stage that consumes structured data and outputs only prose destroys the claim-to-source links. Keeping claims and sources arrays intact, joined by a shared ID with a quote and locator, turns the analysts' review from re-derivation into spot-checking. A bibliography or confidence rating does not say which source supports which figure.

quiz.stem: A research system is asked for the size of the battery-recycling market. One subagent cites a 2024 industry report giving $12B; another cites a 2026 government statistics release giving $9B under a narrower definition. No source settles which definition the requester means, and no data was found for Southeast Asia. Which TWO elements belong in the synthesized output? (Select TWO.)
options: The 2026 figure reported as the answer, since it is the newer source, with the 2024 figure noted in a footnote as superseded.
Both claims with quote, locator, retrieval time, and source date, plus an unresolved conflict annotation naming the human decision needed.
Whichever figure most sources support, after the system searches for additional market reports to settle the disagreement.
The average of the two figures presented as a blended estimate, with both of the sources listed in the references section.
A coverage-gap statement that no Southeast Asia data was found, so that the absence is not read as a zero market there.
quiz.explanation: Given contradictory sources with no basis for choosing, any single figure is wrong as an output because it hides that there is no one answer. The output should carry both claims with their provenance and temporal details, annotate the conflict as unresolved with the human decision named, and state coverage gaps so silence is not read as a finding. Recency, majority vote, and averaging all resolve the conflict silently.

quiz.stem: A support knowledge assistant answers human agents' questions by combining policy PDFs with live results from the order-management tool. Compliance now requires every statement in an answer to be traceable to its exact source. The team has enabled the Citations feature on the policy documents only. What else is needed to meet the requirement?
options: Nothing further is needed, because the citations attached to the answer will also cover statements drawn from order-tool results.
Carry provenance for tool-derived statements in the team's own record structure: tool name, record ID, and retrieval time.
Instruct the model to write a page number in parentheses after every statement, including those based on order-tool results.
Paste the full text of each cited policy page into the answer so reviewers can check every statement against the original.
quiz.explanation: Citations configured on the policy documents return pointers into those documents, with the exact cited passage and a page location, but the order-tool results are not among the cited documents. Where citations do not apply, such as synthesis across tool results, provenance has to be carried in your own record structure. Prompt-based page numbers are less reliable than parsed citation pointers and mean nothing for a tool result.
